By applying partial fraction relations, we were able to simplify the computation of the two-loop Wilson coefficient to a level where it can be evaluated using conventional techniques. This technique has also enabled us to derive a related quantity at two-loop order in a specific gauge, which had previously been difficult to calculate.

This paper focuses on analyzing the chordal nature of the power graph in finite groups. The paper identifies both the groups for which the power graph is chordal - specifically, finite Abelian and finite Nilpotent groups - and the cyclic subgroups within finite groups whose corresponding power graphs are chordal.

The goal of target source separation is to identify and isolate a specific speaker within a conversation, using only a single microphone. This task is crucial for improving speech quality, particularly in distant speakers or those speaking simultaneously. A new method, optimal condition training (OCT), is introduced to enhance the performance of all target source separation techniques, yielding notable improvements. Additionally, a more efficient approach, fast optimal condition training (FOCT), is proposed to reduce computational time, and a more robust variant, robust fast optimal condition training (ROCT), is also developed to enhance its reliability in noisy environments. Experimental results show that OCT and its variants significantly outperform existing methods, yielding up to 2 dB in signal-to-distortion ratio, and demonstrate a linear relationship with the number of speakers, highlighting its potential for practical application.

This research explores the quantum Fisher information in the context of entanglement synchronization. The study reveals how the properties of the entanglement operator affect the quantum Fisher information in block incoherent states, specifically its dependence on the degree of incoherence and entanglement. Additionally, the impact of dephasing channels on the information was investigated. Our findings demonstrate that the entanglement degree plays a crucial role in determining the quantum Fisher information.

Our research examines the behavior of the soft X-ray spectrum in relation to the source size of the X-ray emitting region of the X-ray binary H 1743-322. We utilize the rise and fall phases of the 2017-2019 outburst for our analysis, which is based on data collected from the \emph{Rossi X-ray Telescope} (RXTE) and the \emph{Fermi} Gamma-Ray Space Telescope. We have found that the source size remains consistent throughout the outburst's rise and fall phases, which is around 2-3 km. Furthermore, our results indicate that the frequency dependence of the QPO fractional rms is consistent in both phases, which is consistent with the findings of the 2008 outburst. Notably, our analysis reveals that the source size remains constant across a broad frequency range, which is in line with the expectations of the SSRT model. However, our results also reveal that the frequency dependence of the QPO fractional rms exhibits a distinct pattern in the rise and fall phases, particularly in the low frequency range. Specifically, the QPO fractional rms in the decay phase is lower than that in the rise phase, which is in line with the predictions of the model. This behavior is attributed to the decrease in the source's surface area as the frequency increases.

Extractive question answering systems can be enhanced by modifying pre-trained models to accommodate a pre-defined set of questions against specific document types, thus allowing for tailored representations in languages with fewer resources, such as Romanian. This is achieved by initially training a Romanian language model on a task-agnostic dataset and then fine-tuning it on a question-answering task. The approach's effectiveness is further amplified by utilizing a multilingual pre-trained model that is trained on a variety of languages, including Romanian. The results show that models trained under these conditions can achieve performance comparable to their English-based counterparts in extractive question answering.

The distribution of missing baryons in the universe is closely tied to the structure of galaxy filaments and sheets, as well as the underdense regions known as voids. A new study has analyzed the distribution of missing baryons in the Cosmic Web by comparing the X-ray luminosity of galaxy filaments and sheets to that of voids. The study used data from the XMM-Newton telescope and found that galaxy filaments and sheets have a significantly higher baryonic mass than voids. The team also discovered that the X-ray luminosity of galaxy filaments and sheets increases with their mass, while voids have a significantly lower void thermal X-ray luminosity. The study suggests that galaxy filaments and sheets are the primary locations of missing baryons in the universe, as they have a much higher baryonic mass than voids.

We introduce an algorithm to approximate the treewidth of graphs within a specific constraint. Given an undirected graph and an integer representing the desired treewidth, our method operates in polynomial time, with its execution time directly proportional to the desired treewidth. This is an improvement over previous treewidth approximation algorithms, which had execution times directly proportional to the size of the parameter. Our method is based on a decomposition of the graph and a subsequent analysis of the resulting components.

We have analyzed the optical spectra of 16 TDEs in post-starburst galaxies, which were identified by the Zwicky Transient Facility. Our results show that none of these spectra match the patterns expected of Type Ia supernovae or TDEs. The spectra are more similar to those of galaxies that are in a state of quenching, and this suggests that the observed re-cooling of the gas in these galaxies is occurring. The rate of occurrence of TDEs is estimated to be around 0.3 per year per galaxy, which is significantly lower than the rate of Type Ia supernovae. This discrepancy is more consistent with the rate of TDEs as inferred from the decline of the optical afterglow of a TDE.

In a network of base stations, operating on the Long-Term Evolution of Networks (LTE) standard, a significant problem arises from the base stations' limited number of resource blocks. To address this issue, the base stations must efficiently manage resource block allocation for user equipment requiring continuous connectivity, a task known as dynamic resource block scheduling. The scheduling process is further complicated by the base stations' need to prioritize users with active connections over those in a dormant state. The traditional approach to this problem has been to use fixed scheduling algorithms, but recent studies have shown that these can be improved upon by using machine learning algorithms that allow for the base stations' scheduling decisions to be made based on their observed experience. This paper presents a machine learning-based scheduling algorithm, referred to as the actor-critic learning-based scheduler (ACLS), which uses a deep reinforcement learning method to optimize resource block allocation. The algorithm's performance is evaluated using a detailed simulation study, and the results show that it significantly outperforms traditional scheduling algorithms, achieving a 20% improvement in the base stations' average throughput.

In recent years, word-level quality estimation has gained popularity as a means of automatically assessing sentence quality. This paper conducts a thorough analysis of leading approaches to word-level QE, comparing their performance to sentence-level QE on widely used English and Chinese benchmark datasets. Our results indicate that word-level QE models exhibit different error patterns than sentence-level QE, including variations in performance across specific language scenarios. We propose that word-level QE should primarily be employed to enhance the robustness of translation models rather than being used as a standalone quality metric.

This study focuses on the shadow cast by a new Kerr-de Sitter black hole. This black hole is a result of a four-dimensional topological near-horizon geometry in Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet theory, where a warped product metric is used. Unlike the traditional Kerr-de Sitter shadow, the shadow image of the new black hole exhibits a unique shape and size, with its flatter region near the equator and a more pronounced bulge at the poles. We derive an equation that describes the shadow's shape and utilize a numerical method to obtain its silhouette. Furthermore, the study examines how the gravitational lensing and thermodynamic properties of the black hole change in response to variations in certain parameters.

A novel flux-conservative formulation of relativistic hydrodynamics has been developed to improve upon existing hydrodynamic formulations based on the first-order Godunov method. In this context, the flux function is constructed iteratively from an approximate solution, ensuring that it satisfies the relativistic Euler equations at the point of exit, while also conserving mass, momentum, and energy. This new formulation is demonstrated to yield superior results compared to traditional methods, which often introduce numerical anisotropies and inaccuracies. The advantages of the new flux-conservative formulation are showcased in a series of numerical examples involving shock tube simulations, including one and two-dimensional scenarios.

The $D_{sJ}$ states are primarily characterized by their strong decays into $D^{(*)}K^0_{\rm S}$, and the majority of these states can be explained by an SU(3) flavor symmetry breaking effect. In this study, we investigate the $D_{sJ}$ states through the $D^*_{s2}(2573)^+$ and $D_{sJ}$-mixing mechanisms to understand their natural origins. By analyzing the $D^*_{s2}(2573)^+$ and $D^*_{s1}(2536)^+$, $D^*_{sJ}$ decays into $D^{*}K^0_{\rm S}$, we found that the $D^*_{s1}(2536)^+$ and $D^*_{sJ}$ decays into $D^{*}K^0_{\rm S}$ are consistent with the hypothesis that the $D^*_{s1}(2536)^+$ and $D^*_{sJ}$ are identical particles. We also conclude that the $D^*_{s2}(2573)^+$ is primarily composed of the molecular state $D^*_{s0}(2565)^+\bar{D}^0$ with a small contribution from the $D^*_{s2}(2573)^+$ from an SU(3) flavor symmetry breaking.

We propose a new method for calculating the fractal dimensions of functions defined on the Sierpi\'nski Gasket and similarly structured spaces by leveraging the properties of filters. This method allows for the estimation of several topological invariants, including Hausdorff, Hausdorff-metric, Pythagorean, and Gr\"artner projections.

To evaluate an image question generation model's ability to create insightful and varied questions, we must assess the quality of the questions they produce. However, this can be a challenging task, especially when the questions lack grammatical structure and relevance to the provided image. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that involves guiding the question generation model to produce questions that are more coherent and relevant. By doing so, we aim to improve the quality of the questions by ensuring they adhere to standard grammatical structures. The performance of our guided model is evaluated using a quality-assessment metric, which demonstrates a significant improvement in the efficiency of the question generation model. The source code and pre-trained models can be accessed through a provided repository.

The dark matter halo core size is a crucial unknown in the context of the cuspy vs cuspless dark matter halo matter power spectrum debate. A new study examines the size of the dark matter halo core in isolated galaxies, which determines how the core size is affected by the mass of the halo and the baryonic surface density. The analysis uses a cosmological simulation to determine how the core size is affected by these factors and also investigates how the core size is affected by the mass of the halo in different mass ranges. The study also compares the predictions of the NFW model with those of a model that does not have a core, and finds that the NFW model does not do a good job of predicting the core size for low mass galaxies, but does a good job of predicting the core size for high mass galaxies.

Resolving Boolean satisfiability problems involves a technique called literal elimination, 
wherein a satisfiable formula has a valid model from which a literal is removed, resulting in another satisfiable formula.
Research has shown that in certain situations, this process yields a satisfiable formula faster than random selection.
However, a more effective approach has been discovered, termed quasipure literal elimination, by giving preference to certain 
types of clauses, resulting in a higher success rate, particularly with more complex input formulas, 
leading to a greater average number of derived clauses and shorter running times.

We introduce a novel approach to studying the evolutionary game theoretical properties
of games played by artificial intelligence systems. Our findings indicate that, when
AI systems employ straightforward selection methods, they are likely to converge towards
Nash equilibria in any game scenario. This conclusion is supported by two key points:
firstly, when games involve no mutual benefits, a specific location on the game board
will always yield the best results, while all other areas will result in a loss; secondly,
when games involve conflicting goals, AI systems will consistently work together to
maximize their collective gains.

This research focuses on a multivariate regression tree algorithm, building upon the traditional CART method. The core concept involves using joint probability distributions to represent the relationship between target and feature variables, allowing for a more nuanced approach. The algorithm utilizes a nearest neighbor search to efficiently determine optimal splits by leveraging a sorted cache of axis-aligned hyperrectangles in $O(\log d + \log n)$ time, where $d$ represents the number of dimensions and $n$ represents the number of points. The algorithm also explores the integration of online learning principles, providing a solution that can be applied in a streaming environment. The proposed solution relies on a dynamic data structure that allows for constant-time estimates of multivariate normal distributions, leveraging a modified version of the CDF algorithm to achieve independence between point estimates. The algorithm also allows for the derivation of confidence intervals, providing a basis for quantile error estimation.

This research introduces the concept of censored communication among EV charging algorithms. By implementing a two-tiered approach, where the charging algorithm restricts some battery level measurements to be shared with the grid operator, the system can efficiently manage power demand in real-time. This strategy is beneficial as it enables the charging algorithm to request data only when its battery state necessitates consideration. We propose two power control algorithms that can function under this communication constraint and evaluate their performance relative to a non-censored method. The results indicate that the censored algorithms can effectively balance charging demands with minimal impact on the grid operator's ability to manage peak power usage, ultimately leading to improved system efficiency compared to the non-censored approach.

To assess the predictive power of machine-learning models in predicting electronic properties, we must consider how different density functionals affect these predictions, especially when training and testing data are limited. This issue is addressed by generating datasets using various density functionals for small-molecule systems, where we apply machine-learning models to predict energy differences between molecules and obtain accurate results using a small training set of around 10,000 data points. However, we find that different density functionals yield distinct predictions, highlighting the necessity of pre-training the machine-learning models on a large training set to minimize these discrepancies.

Metagenomic studies have shown that bacterial communities in various environments, like the human gut, differ significantly in species composition, but it remains unclear what factors drive these variations. Using a model that simulates bacterial metabolism and growth in a virtual environment, we discovered that the metabolic capabilities of individual bacteria determine the habitats they occupy within a given ecosystem. We found that the overall metabolic range of a community is influenced more by the availability of nutrients in each habitat than by the total amount of nutrients available in the entire system. Moreover, our model predicted that the metabolic requirements of bacteria in different environments, like the gut and its contents, would differ more than those in different environments, like the gut and mouth. Finally, our model showed that the metabolic structure of a community can be understood by studying the metabolic needs of individual species, rather than taking into account the entire range of metabolic capabilities.

The monitoring of building systems has become increasingly dependent on advanced data analysis techniques, particularly with the widespread use of the KNX protocol in smart buildings. Efficient data processing and visualization are essential for optimal building management. However, dealing with large datasets is a significant challenge, requiring effective methods to minimize processing time. The Symbolic Aggregate Approximation (SAA) approach, which involves aggregating data into symbols, is a promising solution that also enhances the performance of data processing and machine learning algorithms. By integrating SAA with time-series analysis, we have developed an effective method for processing large datasets from building monitoring systems. The proposed approach involves two stages: the SAA-based time-series analysis stage, which aggregates data into symbols, and the symbolic analysis stage, which processes and visualizes the aggregated data. We implemented the proposed method using the open-source KNX4J library to collect data from a smart building, which was then analyzed and visualized using our implementation.

The nature of the progenitors of hydrogen-poor supernovae remains unclear.  A binary system consisting of a relatively cool, low-metallicity star and a more luminous companion with an orbital period of about 10 days is proposed to give rise to the hydrogen-poor supernovae that are associated with the Type Ic-BL class of the Swift-0203014 and ASASSN-15oj types.  This binary system is predicted to produce a mass transfer process that leads to the evolution of the less luminous star.  This binary system is also consistent with the observed characteristics of the host galaxies and the locations of the supernovae in the color-magnitude diagram. The unique properties of two-dimensional magnets are crucial for the development of flexible, non-volatile data storage devices. To better understand the complex behavior of these magnets, we studied the magnetization switching in two-dimensional systems. By analyzing the Stoner-Wohlfarth model, we found that the energy barrier for magnetization switching is influenced by both temperature and the shape of the magnetic domains. When the temperature increases, the switching process becomes more pronounced and the distribution of domain shapes becomes wider. This research provides valuable insights into the magnetization switching mechanism in two-dimensional magnets and can be applied to the prediction and optimization of domain wall dynamics in these systems.

In the field of natural language processing, constituency grammar induction is a crucial task that involves determining the sentence structure. This research focuses on the visual representation of linguistic syntax, utilizing visual region representations to improve the task's performance. We introduce a new dataset called the Visual Constituency Grammar Induction Dataset, containing sentence images and the corresponding constituency trees. This dataset is designed to help researchers develop syntax models that integrate visual information. We also propose a novel syntax model that uses a transformer network to integrate visual region representations into a sequence-to-sequence framework, resulting in significant improvements over existing baseline methods on the VCgid dataset.

A new method is presented to gauge the reliability of attribution techniques by comparing their results on a single dataset against those on multiple unrelated datasets. This approach assesses attribution methods' performance across different datasets and demonstrates that some metrics consistently correlate well, while others fail to generalize. This metric's implementation and corresponding results on a range of datasets are discussed, along with potential applications and further ideas for research.

We explore the concept of double shadows in the context of static, spherically symmetric wormholes that have the same gravitational effect as a black hole of mass $M$. We investigate the conditions under which a black hole and a white hole are observed, and how this observation changes in the case of wormhole photons. We analyze the parameter space that results in double shadows and find that certain black hole metrics produce double shadows for all photon orbits. We also examine the effects of a wormhole's throat geometry and photon geodesics on the observed shadow and find that the shape, size, and duration of double shadows are highly sensitive to the metric used to describe the wormhole throat.

This research paper builds on a previously established subadditivity estimate for permutations of matrices with positive entries by Bener and Ronu by applying it to matrices with nonnegative entries, thereby providing a valuable tool for making permanent approximations. We demonstrate the utility of our findings by establishing new approximation estimates for the permanent of specific matrices with nonnegative entries, notably for triangular matrices, matrices with a single positive row or column, and zero matrices augmented with a single nonnegative entry above the diagonal.

By employing transfer matrices and free fermion techniques, some characteristics of the model are examined in detail. This paper addresses the challenge of single or multiple target tracking in scenarios where the target's characteristics are unknown. A proposed approach utilizes a conditional variational autoencoder to differentiate between target instances within the same class and those from unknown sources. By training this model with a combination of labeled and unlabeled target data, it learns to represent target features in a latent space where similarities between known targets are maximized and unknown targets are minimized. In the prediction phase, targets are classified as known or unknown based on their latent representation similarity with training targets. Experimental evaluations were conducted using the SMAPC dataset, and results demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in distinguishing target origins in various scenarios.

This research presents a novel 3D vehicle reconstruction method that leverages a single RGB image for a single-view input. The approach combines a two-branch Convolutional Neural Network and a graph-based optimization technique to refine the vehicle shape. The first network branch generates a preliminary vehicle shape, while the second branch refines this shape by focusing on wheel and body relationships. The optimization method, based on a geometric graph, further enhances the vehicle's geometry by connecting wheels and bodies. The method also incorporates soft shape constraints to regularize the vehicle shape, yielding accurate 3D reconstructions. Extensive testing across multiple datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach, with source code available on GitHub.

This research introduces a pioneering approach to automatically generating query graphs 
that complement visual query languages. By combining a query graph with text and spatial information, 
it facilitates seamless interaction between visual and textual platforms. We have developed two 
groundbreaking network architectures: one for generating query graphs given natural language 
descriptions and the other for predicting query tree lexicograms given query graphs. Our proposed 
method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in spatial reasoning from natural language 
and yields a notable enhancement of 7.5% in F1-score on the Visual Question Answering Dataset.
This paper outlines a novel approach to developing cryptosystems that operate on an infinite character set and are adaptable to numerous alphabets.

Accurately identifying and linking named entities to corresponding entities in a knowledge graph is a crucial task for knowledge graph construction and retrieval. We introduce a novel, data-driven approach called Entity Fusion that optimizes named entity disambiguation and linking. This method combines two primary strategies: resolving ambiguities based on graph structures and relying on information extracted from content available online. We evaluate Entity Fusion in the context of DBpedia and Wikidata, and it successfully achieves high accuracy rates in both named entity disambiguation and entity linking.

In the electroweak Standard Model, the one-loop corrections to the gauge bosons' self-energy, as described by their S, T, and U parameters, are extensively analyzed. By employing the Passarino-Veltman method, the momentum-space expressions for the bosonic self-energies are systematically computed, thereby validating the previously derived momentum-space formulas for the S, T, and U parameters. The derived results are shown to align perfectly with the corresponding momentum-space expressions derived from direct application of the electroweak Ward identities to the bosonic two-loop vacuum diagrams.

Recent advances in deep dynamic scene understanding have led to the development of neural view synthesis, enabling realistic image generation from brief video inputs. Nonetheless, learning these implicit functions in isolation is often challenging due to the absence of supplementary data or supervision signals. In this research, we propose a novel regularization approach for learning neural view synthesis using unsupervised techniques derived from self-consistency and motion fields. Through experimentation, we demonstrate that these auxiliary signals derived from supplementary information are not necessary and that the loss functions themselves can serve as effective inputs for generating images from a single video. Our results demonstrate that the combination of these signals can yield comparable performance to more complex methods relying on supplementary data or supervision.

We establish the solution $Y$ to a specific differential equation as a branched rough path with a regularity of $3/2$. The approach begins with demonstrating that the solution's approximation, with a higher regularity, specifically $\gamma=3/3/5$ for the rough driver $B$, is unique, and we then derive a specific inequality for the solution's approximation, with a higher regularity, specifically $\gamma=3/5$. This uniqueness result and approximation inequality enable us to prove the required regularity of the solution $Y$.

This research explores the application of a novel framework for analyzing the asymptotic properties of nonlinear functions of random grain models, particularly those of limited variable range. The study provides an explicit expression for the asymptotic form of the probability function and subsequent asymptotic properties for functions like minimum, maximum, and order statistics. The findings are supported by the use of relevant and applicable asymptotic expansions based on the asymptotic form of the probability density function and its derivatives. Furthermore, the research derives and presents asymptotic expansions for the cumulative distribution function and moments of the functions. Additionally, the study establishes connections between the asymptotic properties of nonlinear functions and those of the underlying random grain models, including the applicability of Mehler's formula and Charlier polynomials.

A relatively new technology known as a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS) has the potential to revolutionize the way future wireless networks operate. RIS-assisted networks, which rely on a network-attached RIS for communication, have garnered significant interest due to their capabilities. Despite this interest, various challenges to implementing these networks in real-world scenarios persist. The first hurdle is the need for machine learning algorithms that can efficiently manage RIS user equipment (UE) channel estimation. In this study, a novel framework for online channel estimation is introduced, which utilizes a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method to optimize the transmission of pilot sequences and the estimation process. The framework is designed to minimize the mean squared error (MSE) of RIS-UE channels, and its performance is evaluated under different transmission protocols, including time division duplex (TDD) and frequency division duplex (FDD) methods. The framework is further tested in an environment with changing RIS configurations, where a new online learning strategy is implemented to update the trained model. The results demonstrate that this framework can achieve competitive performance compared to existing methods, even in complex communication systems.

We introduce a novel approach to simplify complex stochastic systems. This method
involves collapsing the system's detailed dynamics into a simplified continuous-time
Markov chain, allowing for accurate predictions of key system properties. The
method's computational efficiency is impressive, requiring only a single system
simulation and some pre-computation to provide reliable estimates. The accuracy
of these predictions is remarkable, as they capture the full range of possible
outcomes, not just their average characteristics. The utility of this method
is demonstrated in various applications, including the analysis of genetic
recombination, virus dynamics, and protein degradation, and comparing different
receptor models. By transforming a system with many hidden states into one
with just a few, our approach offers a more interpretable model that still
retains its predictive power.

The performance of deep learning models can be improved by reducing the bit depth of the models, but this results in a decrease in accuracy. Our approach, called cyclic training (CiTrain), helps to minimize this loss in accuracy, particularly for models with extremely low-bit quantization. CiTrain involves alternating between highly accurate and highly quantized versions of the model, where the accurate version has a higher bit depth than the quantized one. This technique can be applied to various low-bit quantized neural networks. CiTrain was tested on two well-known networks, MobileNetV2 and ResNet50, and compared to other state-of-the-art quantization methods across various bit widths. The results show that CiTrain produces models with better performance and smaller sizes than baseline methods, while maintaining efficient inference and training processes.

Theoretical predictions suggest that white dwarf mergers may produce a significant portion of Type Ia supernovae.  The progenitor conditions for these events are still uncertain, particularly with regards to the single degenerate channel of white dwarf collisions.  To shed light on these conditions, we employed a population synthesis model to investigate the properties of white dwarf collision systems.  The results indicate that the single degenerate channel of white dwarf collisions occurs in the densest regions of globular clusters and the outer regions of dwarf galaxies.  The model suggests that the collisions in these areas are likely the result of core collapse, rather than core expansion.  The predicted mass of the white dwarf collision systems is approximately 0.2-0.3 solar masses.  The model also suggests that the collisions in these areas are likely to produce Type Ia supernovae with low explosion energies and high helium content.  The predicted rate of Type Ia supernovae from white dwarf collisions in globular clusters is approximately 0.1-0.3% per year, while the rate in dwarf galaxies is approximately 0.01-0.1% per year.  The model also suggests that the rate of Type Ia supernovae from white dwarf collisions in the Milky Way is approximately 0.001-0.0018 solar mass per year. In the context of online learning with a fixed model architecture, we investigate
the challenges posed by training data that is incrementally revealed in small
portions. We develop an approach to optimize the order of presenting training
chunks to enhance learning performance. We demonstrate that this optimization
problem can be reformulated as a variant of the Knapsack Problem and solve
it heuristically. We then introduce a simple strategy to expedite training by
diversifying the order of training chunks. We validate the efficacy of our
methods through numerical simulations and highlight their practical relevance.

A new concept, Digital Vaccine Passport, is being used by some governments to manage the ongoing pandemic. It involves assigning and managing a unique digital identity to each individual for vaccine administration, providing updated vaccination records. However, implementing such a system poses significant challenges, including verifying claims, managing large databases, maintaining data integrity, ensuring user anonymity, and preventing data breaches. To overcome these challenges, we propose a decentralized digital vaccine passport system that utilizes blockchain and smart contracts. The system is open-source, transparent, and verifiable, enabling efficient, secure, and private management of vaccination records. We also introduce a mechanism to prevent fraud and preserve user anonymity. The system's effectiveness is demonstrated through a case study on Indonesia, which has faced considerable difficulties in managing their vaccine distribution, a problem faced by many countries. The proposed solution offers a viable solution to address the complex challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic.

This study examines the connection between clustering in sentence embeddings and categories in text datasets, exploring whether distinct classes yield separate clusters. We develop a method to automatically categorize topic classes based on the similarity of their embeddings in a learned space and evaluate its effectiveness across multiple benchmarks. Our findings confirm that various pre-trained models achieve substantial performance on these tasks, even in the absence of explicit training for unsupervised topic discovery. This suggests that pre-trained models can be adapted to uncover text subject matters without supervised training.

We explore the diffusion dynamics of a random system comprising N particles in a one-dimensional, discrete lattice framework. Each particle's movement is determined by a time-independent, site-specific probability distribution that adheres to a normalization condition. The particles are non-interacting, with no influence from a potential. We derive the effective diffusion coefficient D(N) as a function of the normalization condition's parameter alpha, with the assumption that the parameter is sufficiently large. The derived expression, $D_N(\alpha)$, depends on the first moment of the particles' distribution, $\bar{x}$. We observe that the effective diffusion coefficient and the localization scale are inversely related. We find that the particles' movement is characterized by a power-law distribution with an exponent $\beta(N,\alpha)$ that depends on the particles' number N and the parameter $\alpha$. We derive the expression for the power-law exponent $\beta(N,\alpha)$ and find that it decreases with an increase in the particles' number N. We also find that the particles' variance $\sigma^2(N,\alpha)$ is proportional to the power-law expression $D_N\beta_N\alpha$. We also derive the expression for the mean time $\tau(N,\alpha)$ for the particles' localization, with the result that it is proportional to the power-law expression $D_N\beta_N\alpha$. We also find that the particles' movement is characterized by a power-law distribution in the particles' time-of-flight distribution.

The spin relaxation process through interactions with nuclei is a critical aspect of magnetic resonance imaging, with a primary mechanism being the interaction between protons and $^{19}$C nuclei in diamond. In contrast to previously studied phenomena, this effect has a unique time-dependence that is not constant over time. We employed a computational approach based on density matrix analysis to model this effect and found that it is heavily influenced by the system's hyperfine interaction parameters. We also found that this effect is highly dependent on the frequency mismatch between $^{13}$C and $^{19}$C, allowing for a potential reduction in this relaxation via careful frequency tuning.

We studied the thermalization behavior of a specific type of model, the 2D melon model, which is a periodically driven version of a well-known theory. This model is known for its conformal invariance, and we found that its thermalization behavior is unique. Below a certain point in time, the probability that the system has returned to its initial state decreases over time while its energy density decreases even faster, indicating a certain level of thermalization. However, after this point in time, the system's behavior deviates from these expectations and instead approaches the expected behavior for a system that has fully thermalized, rather than returning to its initial state.

This letter examines the relationship between compressed sensing and multimodal sensor fusion. An algorithm that can identify the most effective sensors for a particular task is presented and its potential application to fusion is explored. An experimental setup was used to test the algorithm's performance, and the results showed significant parallelization benefits. These results have implications for sensor selection in fusion and contribute to the growing connection between compressed sensing and multimodal techniques.

The precise prediction of the $C=\pm1$ phase shift in the $K^0-\bar K^0$ system within the context of the Standard Model is a crucial benchmark for any new physics that may contribute to the system's dynamics. This is particularly relevant for the study of $K^0-\bar K^0$ mixing, as it has been found that the main source of the system's $CP$-violating phase is the work of tree-level weak interactions. As such, this phase shift is a valuable tool in distinguishing between the hypothetical light scalar particles, $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$, which are proposed in the $Z'$ and LHS models of the Standard Model, as they offer alternative explanations for the system's $CPT$ symmetry. This is achieved through a detailed analysis of the system's direct $CP$ violation parameters, which are derived from the study of the $K_L, K_S$ asymmetry differences. This is further supported by the use of the $K_S \to \pi^+\pi^-$ decay amplitude, which is a useful indicator of the system's $CPT$ symmetry.

This research investigates the challenge of achieving a desirable equilibrium in a decentralized system with multiple agents, despite the system's state being imperfectly estimated. A balance exists between communication efficiency, accuracy, and overall system performance, and we seek to find optimal solutions that balance these competing goals. To address this, we establish a theoretical framework that combines the system's performance with the cost of communication and estimation, and we examine the trade-offs that arise from this unified approach. Our analysis reveals the relationship between communication, estimation, and performance, and it indicates that under certain conditions, optimal outcomes can be achieved with reduced communication costs. We illustrate our framework with two examples: a distributed system for estimating states with noisy measurements, and a system for distributed channel selection in cognitive radio networks. The results show that our approach can lead to improved outcomes with reduced communication costs.

This study examines the application of the Gibbs sampler to generate labeled multi-Bernoulli birth distribution for multi-sensor systems. The main objective is to determine the probability of detection (Pd) for each target at a sensor and to identify the origin of measurements indicating target presence. The proposed method uses a Markov chain Monte Carlo approach, where the target birth distribution is updated based on measurements from sensors. The Gibbs sampler combines a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and the Gibbs sampling method to update the target birth distribution based on measurements from sensors. The method iteratively updates the target birth distribution and the sensor detection probability, before generating new target locations based on the updated detection probability, all while keeping track of detection uncertainty. The method's performance is evaluated using a simulation study and is compared with a recently introduced method, the particle Gibbs sampler.

In this study, we investigate how interconnected features can be represented as a network within a linguistic knowledge base. By examining relationships between knowledge attributes, new inquiries emerge beyond those addressed by standard query languages. We identify two key tasks arising from this perspective: determining the closeness of linguistic characteristics and identifying interconnected features. To address these questions, we design a predictive model that identifies relationships between features within a knowledge base by leveraging the correlations between features as nodes in a graph, where edges represent co-occurrence in a sample dataset of languages. By training our model on a knowledge base and an associated annotation dataset, we demonstrate its ability to improve the accuracy of filling missing information in the knowledge base. We further explore the utility of our model for generating novel knowledge, by using it to predict the value of a feature for a language with limited knowledge, and also illustrate how it can be employed to suggest new relationships between features, thus expanding the knowledge base.

We examine the statistical properties of Off-Policy Evaluation (OPE) methods,
assessing their performance in terms of bias, variance, and coverage probability.
To achieve this, we develop asymptotic theory for various advanced OPE methods,
including the Double Robust and Cross-Entropy methods. We also derive a general
statistical framework applicable to a broad range of OPE methods, which can be
used to analyze other methods not covered in the study.
Our analysis yields several key findings: Firstly, we demonstrate that the
Double Robest estimator is a highly efficient estimator under a broad range of
conditions. Secondly, we identify the optimal power balance between bias and
variance for Cross-Entropy methods, and show that it is independent of the
underlying data distribution. Thirdly, we establish that the optimal performance
of OPE methods, measured by bias and coverage probability, is directly linked to
the quality of the data used to estimate context and reward variables, and that
this performance degrades significantly when these variables are poorly estimated.
Our results are further validated through simulations and a real-world case study.

The traditional method of calculating expected earnings from fermentation production often relies on inaccurate assumptions of a normal distribution, which can lead to an underestimation of output variability and a subsequent misunderstanding of expected earnings. This paper presents a novel Bayesian approach to mitigate this issue and offers a robust estimation method for determining expected earnings from an abnormal distribution. The proposed method is then applied to a real-world case study of ethanol production to showcase its practical value.

The polaron problem is solved exactly through a transformation that reveals a connection to a well-studied harmonic problem. The result shows that the mass term resulting from this transformation corresponds to the effective mass of a classical particle, while the polaron wave function can be expressed as a superposition of eigenstates whose coefficients satisfy an ordinary differential equation. By using numerical methods, we are able to analyze systems with arbitrary interactions that involve multiple particles, as well as variable numbers of dimensions and degrees of freedom, something that other polaron theory methods cannot do. Our results are verified through comparisons with variational calculations that use the same basis as our method, showing a strong correlation in the interaction potential and eigenenergies.

The electric flux tube's lifetime is determined when it loses magnetic energy.  In a force-free electrodynamics environment, this loss occurs at a rate proportional to the 1/2 power of the magnetic field strength.  Consequently, the magnetic field strength increases at a rate that is 1/4 times the rate of electric flux decay.  As a result, the magnetic field approaches a 3/4 power solution, which is a well-known result.  However, this paper demonstrates that a 3/4 power solution is unstable and eventually decays to a 1/4 power solution, which is a stable equilibrium.  This 1/4 power solution has significant implications for the magnetic field's behavior in the solar atmosphere, particularly in the context of sunspots and coronal loops.

Schr\"odinger's cat is in a quantum state of superposition, representing both alive and dead at the same time. When observed, this condition collapses into a single state. The cat's ability to be observed can be represented by a probability of being observed, which is governed by a specific equation. The cat's probability of being observed is initially at 100%, but it eventually drops to 0% after an extended period of time. This research aims to examine the properties of minimal periodic and almost periodic decompositions in discrete sequences. We investigate how the length of these decompositions relates to the patterns present and how certain conjectures hold under various levels of complexity. Specifically, we focus on Szabados's conjecture and its generalization by Berlinkov, as well as Gelfond's conjecture. By utilizing techniques from the theory of linear periodic continued fractions and the Frobenius equation, we develop new methods to address these conjectures and provide a deeper understanding of their implications. Moreover, we demonstrate the existence of decompositions that satisfy certain growth conditions by employing the theory of subharmonic functions.

The Gromov-Hausdorff distance serves as a continuous equivalent of equivalence relations among bounded metric spaces. It conveys information about the size and geometric characteristics of a bounded metric space. In the context of Riemannian manifolds, the GH-distance has been extensively studied. This study focuses on a more general target, bounded Ricci curvature averages, and demonstrates that it converges to a true L^2 distance in a specific geometric limit. Moreover, a corresponding moduli space metric is defined, and an analysis of its asymptotic behavior in relation to the space's volume and geometric features, such as first Betti numbers, is presented.

We examine the resolvent of the operator $A$ plus the remainder term $B$ in problems with divergence form. Given that $A$ is a bounded operator plus the fractional Laplacian, we show that for small $\varepsilon$ the remainder term contributes at least to the order of $\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}$. We use this to demonstrate the existence of a weak solution to the nonhomogeneous problem $A u = f$ given certain assumptions on $f$ and domain $\Omega$ which can be a bounded domain or $\mathbb{R}^N$.

In this study, we examine the advantages of using explicit dialogue states, as opposed to training models without them in a task-oriented environment. We utilize the multi-domain dialogue management framework by FoehnixDM to create a data set annotated with explicit states. Our analysis shows that integrating formal dialogue states enhances model performance and allows for a more straightforward creation of a skill-based system framework. We also investigate the benefits of training models with a dialogue management language in a multi-domain setting, where a single general goal is shared across domains, and multiple specific goals are managed within each domain.

A significant number of applications rely heavily on SMT solvers for resolving satisfiability problems.  However, the processing speed of these solvers can be hindered by the time it takes to load data from memory.  This paper proposes Smt-Switch, a technique that enhances the performance of SMT-based applications by preloading key tracks to their stack before invoking the solver, thereby reducing memory access times.  By integrating Smt-Switch with existing SMT libraries, applications can benefit from its improvements without requiring substantial code modifications.  Formal analysis and experimental results validate the effectiveness of Smt-Switch in accelerating the memory access speed, leading to notable performance enhancements in applications that frequently use SMT, achieving an average speedup of 2.6x and a maximum speedup of 5.1x on the Z3 compiler.

The recent development of the Orthogonal Polynomial Projection Quantization (OPPQ) method for precisely calculating the eigenvalues and states of the Morse potential has been built upon previous research on exponential attenuation, yielding a more efficient algorithm. This work is now applied to the study of quasi-exactly solvable states in the Morse potential, yielding accurate results for the eigenvalues and states of the system. Notably, the OPPQ method demonstrates enhanced stability and faster convergence when calculating quasi-exactly solvable states compared to non-quasi-exactly solvable states. This improvement can be attributed to the method's ability to project the potential onto the orthogonal polynomials in the OPPQ expansion, effectively eliminating the singularities present in the non-quasi-exactly solvable states. The method's performance is validated by comparing its results to the exact solutions and other numerical methods. This work is accompanied by a technical discussion of the method's limitations and potential for application to other complex systems.

Deep neural networks are typically trained with a fixed input resolution and this method has been widely adopted. However, researchers have found that retraining a model with different input resolutions allows it to learn multiple levels of abstraction simultaneously. This approach, known as network morphing, can be achieved through domain scaling and patch mixing. An alternative method, known as network morphing with zooming, involves changing the input resolution of a model after it has been initialized. While previous studies have experimented with combining multiple models, each with their own unique input resolution, our proposed method, called ScaleNet, offers a more efficient solution by modifying the input resolution of a single model to achieve different capabilities. ScaleNet's effectiveness is enhanced by a two-stage training process that first pre-trains the model with a fixed input resolution, and then fine-tunes it with a variable resolution. Additionally, we propose a data augmentation technique that increases the model's robustness to input variations and improves its accuracy. ScaleNet's benefits include a lower computational cost, fewer model parameters, and the ability to achieve superior accuracy without sacrificing accuracy in the original task.

Observations of granular convection on Venus, a phenomenon seen in clouds, have sparked debate over the rotation rate of its secondary component, V2094 Tau, a star in the $\beta$ Pictoris moving group. The observations of granular motion on Venus, which suggests a rotation period of 160-200 hours, align with an estimated mass range of 0.5-0.3 solar masses for V2094 Tau, a possibility that challenges the current understanding of the moving group due to the mass ratio issue.

We examine the existence of charged scalar clouds in the vicinity of Schwarzschild black holes with self-interacting potentials of a specific kind. These potentials allow for a unique parameter range where scalar clouds can persist, even in the presence of Gauss-Bonnet gravity. Our analysis involves numerically solving coupled nonlinear equations, derived from the Dirac-Born-Infeld equations in a spherically symmetric, static context. We also derive weak bounds on the charged scalar field's profile, using a Gauss-Bonnet version of Vaidya's outgoing wave solution.

We investigate the potential of $\mu\mu\to ee$ coherent scattering of neutrinos
as a novel source of flavor tagging to investigate the active-sterile neutrino
oscillation theory. We consider the scenario where a sterile neutrino with a mass of
approximately 10 MeV, consistent with the $\tau$ radiative decay invisibility, undergoes
coherent scattering with an electron beam. We determine the likelihood of observing
the event's presence or absence, and also explore the possibility of measuring the
CP-violating phases associated with the sterile neutrino with a 90% confidence level.
The study concludes that a future muon-to-electron collider, capable of producing 1000
pairs per day, may be capable of detecting the event with a 90% confidence level, and
also have the potential to measure the CP-violating phases associated with the sterile
neutrino with a 90% confidence level.

We present a new image restoration model that effectively removes noise and
artifacts from images using a combination of unsupervised learning techniques.
The model consists of three key components: a CVF module that separates clean
images from noisy input data, a feature reconstruction module that reconstructs
clean image features, and a generator that generates the denoised images. We
introduce a cycle consistency constraint to ensure the output of the model is
close to the original clean image. This approach allows for the efficient
training of all modules in a single end-to-end pipeline. Experimental results
across various datasets demonstrate the robustness and versatility of the model.

We address the challenge of recovering a k-sparse signal from an underdetermined system of equations, where the unknown matrix A is randomly generated. The solution must be not only precise but also efficient in terms of time complexity. Our work builds on the existing theory of sparse recovery and offers a probabilistic upper bound on the number of rows required for matrix A, provided the signal's support can be recovered with high probability. This bound is tighter than existing bounds by a factor of at least $(\log N)^{2.5},$ and it is also applicable to signals with a binary pattern. Furthermore, we establish a corresponding lower bound, up to a logarithmic factor, on the number of rows needed to achieve the same level of certainty in the recovery of A.

This paper explores the use of higher-order contracts in a type system that supports union and intersection types, reviewing existing type systems for first-order contracts and adapting them to work with higher-order contracts, demonstrating the increased complexity of combining these features with union and intersection types, along with an implementation in the Rastellini calculus.

In the realm of reinforcement learning, especially in real-world scenarios where rewards are scarce, developing agents that can function effectively is a significant challenge. To tackle this, we have designed a novel algorithm known as Reward Augmentation (RA), which leverages intrinsic motivation combined with extrinsic rewards to train and evaluate the proposed agents. RA achieves this by iteratively augmenting the original sparse reward signal with a novel reward function, which is derived from the agent's behavior in the current episode, and scaling it. Through our experiments, RA has demonstrated its ability to significantly enhance the training efficiency of state-of-the-art RL algorithms in multiple domains, including environments with grid-based and continuous representations. Furthermore, RA has shown its capability to generalize to unseen domains, highlighting its potential to tackle complex real-world challenges.

We investigate the oscillatory behavior of a particle subject to an anharmonic potential, and observe that its motion can be described by a damped periodic process. The total energy of the particle is conserved during this motion. We find that a perturbative series expansion of the particle's motion can be accurately represented by a hyperbolic cosine function, whose coefficients correlating to terms in the series expansion are found to be the renormalized frequencies of the oscillatory motion. We derive a formula to calculate these frequencies, and note that they are analogous to the frequencies obtained from the normal modes of a system. We propose that these frequencies are the natural frequencies of the anharmonic oscillator, and provide evidence that they are independent of initial conditions. We also show that the period of the particle's motion is closely approximated by the minimum time required for it to complete an oscillatory cycle.

We investigate the two-point correlation functions of a scalar and graviton in general higher derivative gravity theories, focusing on their UV properties. By examining contributions from three key topologies, we identify a complex interplay of terms, leading to a cancellation of UV divergences in geometric functions. Notably, our analysis reveals that while geometric functions vanish in the point limit, correlation functions do not. Additionally, our work highlights the importance of a specific derivative order in determining the UV behavior of these theories, a finding with significant implications for theories with higher derivative terms.

The widespread adoption of social media has made it a valuable resource for researchers, whose work is being driven by the vast potential for data-driven insights. However, as users continuously generate content, rule-breaking also tends to increase. Studies have demonstrated that users who are suspended from platforms tend to be more disruptive than their active peers, but previous studies have been hindered by the lack of access to suspended users' data. We have addressed this limitation by creating a dataset of 1.3 million suspended users' tweets, collected during the 2010-2019 timeframe, along with 2.2 million control samples from the same timeframes. Our comprehensive analysis reveals a notable disparity between suspended and active users, with suspended users exhibiting higher rates of rule-breaking than expected, including increased toxicity, abuse, and hate speech, along with a higher propensity for spreading misinformation and engaging in sensationalized content. Furthermore, our regression models demonstrate that suspended users' content is characterized by lower quality and greater negativity, and exhibits a greater impact on the platform due to its influence on engagement and feedback. Our research highlights the importance of large-scale, high-quality datasets in better understanding online behavior and its implications for content moderation.

The EIC and FCC-hh projects represent two major research initiatives that require advanced accelerators, specifically, the EIC may employ existing or future accelerators, whereas the FCC-hh will utilize two separate accelerators, each operating at different energy levels. Implementing an EIC experiment could benefit from testing the capabilities of the FCC-hh accelerators, while also enabling the development of a future hadron-hadron collider based on the successful EIC project.

This research introduces an innovative approach to neural network training in scenarios where labels are uncertain. By integrating data from multiple networks with varying parameters and applying a strategy to stabilize learning, we demonstrate that a consensus model can achieve higher accuracy than individual networks. The performance of our method is compared to other approaches in a well-known dataset, and we provide a theoretical analysis to support its effectiveness.

This study examines the prioritization of resource allocation in V2X communications for safety-critical vehicles under conditions of limited spectrum. A new resource allocation mechanism is proposed that prioritizes crash-prone vehicles by utilizing vehicular channel state information, and this is evaluated using stochastic game theory. The evaluation shows that the new mechanism offers superior performance over existing methods, and numerical simulations confirm that it can effectively reduce the time to transmit safety messages by nearly 50% in high-risk traffic scenarios compared to current standards.

The rapid advancement of AI technologies has sparked concerns over their ethical implications, leading to a heightened focus on the need for social responsibility in various fields. As AI continues to permeate society, ensuring transparency and accountability are crucial, especially in the social and emotional impact of these systems. We are exploring ways to address these concerns by developing a framework that integrates affective computing principles with social responsibility frameworks. This research aims to identify key effects and assessment methods for emotional AI systems, drawing from the knowledge of experts in the field through qualitative analysis of established frameworks and literature review. We aim to contribute to the development of responsible AI by providing a comprehensive framework that can be applied across industries, sectors, and age groups to guide the design of AI systems that prioritize emotional well-being.

In this study, we investigate how using feature toggles impacts the process of merging code branches. Our analysis is based on a comprehensive dataset of 1.8 million changes from 25 projects, including 1,000,000+ branch merges. Our findings reveal that incorporating feature toggles indeed reduces the number of code merges, and this is primarily due to the delayed integration of new features. Moreover, we found that projects utilizing feature toggles exhibit a notable decline in merges with a high degree of confidence – at least one in every 50 changes.

The Navier-Stokes equations in two and three dimensions display a concept of emergent symmetry, which results in the conservation of vorticity and enstrophy. This phenomenon is linked to an accidental symmetry within these equations. Building upon this, we have found a novel accidental symmetry within the vorticity equation, which could potentially secure the conservation of enstrophy. This potential symmetry is based on an inverse relation between a fluid's vorticity and the velocity gradient tensor's eigenvalues. This relationship holds across all fluid flows and is not affected by external forces or boundaries. Consequently, it represents a conserved quantity under all fluid flows. The discovery of this symmetry may offer new insights into the behavior of turbulent flows and the behavior of vortices in fluid dynamics.

We propose a versatile, modular framework to illustrate the internal workings of convolutional neural networks, which can be applied across various tasks and models. By leveraging the Cephalomach learning algorithm, we derive a mathematical representation of network filters in terms of input patterns and activation levels. To facilitate comprehension, we employ the mathematical model to transform filter expressions into 3D visualizations, providing insight into both the specific input features being detected and the corresponding confidence assigned by the network. Utilizing the expression-based approach, we successfully apply our framework to a range of tasks, including image classification, segmentation, and object detection, and explore how the network's features evolve during the training process. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of our visualization method in network pruning, showcasing its ability to reveal the specific input features being discarded. To enhance the analysis, we also introduce the Maximum Attention visualization, which provides a comprehensive overview of the network's focus on specific input features.

We present calculations of loop effects incorporating new massive spin-2 fields within the framework of high-energy particle physics. By employing a Dirac-Born-Infeld action, the interactions of these massive spin-2 fields with the graviton are established. Their impact on the gravitational interaction vertex is also determined, along with a derivation of the self-energy correction to graviton propagator. This allows us to calculate the loop-corrected graviton propagator in both vacuum and Hadamard states. By utilizing the vacuum state, the scattering amplitude involving gravitons and massive spin-2 fields is calculated, along with a derivation of the one-loop beta function for their coupling to gravity. This beta function reveals that the coupling exhibits infrared divergence, leading to two possible infrared regimes. Our findings are compared with the IR regime of string theory. Additionally, the scattering amplitude involving gravitons and massive spin-2 fields within the Hadamard state is calculated, along with a derivation of the one-loop correction to graviton propagator in this framework. This reveals that the one-loop correction to graviton propagator is independent of infrared divergence.

The peace vs war dilemma is a complex issue, as the outcome is uncertain and influenced by multiple factors, including the adversary's intentions and capabilities, as well as the negotiator's own strength and bargaining power. Each party's perception of this situation is shaped by their own political bias, leading to a unique and subjective perspective on the war-pacifism spectrum. This paper proposes a model that captures the negotiator's peace or war decision, based on their bias, resulting in four possible scenarios: a biased negotiator opting for war, or opting for peace. The paper then examines the relationships between these outcomes and the negotiator's bias, as well as the impact of their bias on the negotiation process. The model also explores the relationship between bias and the negotiator's expected outcome, and the effectiveness of negotiations in achieving peace.

When we process sentences, our brain combines instantiations of
meaning combined through unique neural patterns, a phenomenon previously observed
in studies of sentence priming. This study investigates the neural basis of
sentence understanding, particularly how related filling patterns overlap across
different conditions. We examined 26 native English speakers in a task where they
identified the correct object that fit into the starting phrase of a sentence,
given two possible options. The sentences were either about actions, like "She
is placing the book on the desk," or not, such as "She is placing the book on the
wall." We recorded the brain activity of our subjects using fMRI and analyzed
neural patterns using multivariate pattern analysis. Our results showed that the
brain regions responsible for object filling overlap more when the initial
patterns are related to actions, as opposed to those that aren't. This pattern was
consistent with predictions from neurocognitive theories that suggest
action-related patterns are more fundamental and shared across different
conditions in sentence understanding.

The detection of gravitational waves through laser interferometers like LIGO, LISA, and LIGO India relies heavily on their ability to precisely measure wave patterns using optical interferometers. However, the current angular resolution of these machines is limited by the available data, at approximately 10 degrees. To improve this, we're working on a project that utilizes artificial neural networks to enhance the angular precision of these gravitational wave detectors. By training our model on a dataset of simulated gravitational wave events, we've been able to significantly reduce the angular resolution, down to 0.1 degrees. This is crucial for the accurate timing and localization of triggers, which is essential for the successful operation of these gravitational wave detectors.

The spatial Point Spread Function (PSF) of an optical telescope exhibits a complex nature resulting from the interplay between the primary mirror's seeing and wavefront errors. To model the spatial PSD, we utilize a two-dimensional expansion of the PSF, incorporating a conditional probability distribution that accounts for the interplay between seeing and wavefront errors. By incorporating a prior seeing distribution into the conditional probability model, we generate a conditional spatial PSD. Our proposed method is validated through a simulation involving a 8-meter diameter telescope with a seeing of 0.6 arcseconds and an average wavefront error of 60 nm, with the spatial PSD being calculated for both the total and the conditional responses.

The accuracy of phonon dispersion is crucial for understanding both static and dynamic properties of solids. Density functional theory, often utilized in solid-state calculations, is commonly applied for predicting phonon frequencies. Nevertheless, previous studies have encountered difficulties in achieving agreement with experimental data, particularly when considering van der Waals interactions. To address this challenge, we have developed a new approach that combines the r2SCAN density functional with the quasi-harmonic deformation model to predict phonon frequencies. This method was tested on various materials with diverse structures, including molecules, low-dimensional systems, ionic solids, and metallic solids. The results demonstrate that our approach consistently yields phonon frequencies in close agreement with experimental findings. This breakthrough offers a new tool for reliable phonon calculations in a wide range of materials.

This paper proposes a universal technique to calculate coverability sets of very-WSTS under certain conditions. Within this framework, it is demonstrated that the coverability sets of very-WSTS can be defined as the least solution to a system of polynomial equations. The method is applied to a class of very-WSTS characterized by polynomial transition semigroups. This includes a significant subset of Petri nets, for which coverability sets can be determined algorithmically.

The Broad Emission Line region in Active Galactic Nuclei exhibits significant variability over short periods but poses difficulties when studying long-term changes. 
Recent AGN monitoring efforts have been made possible by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey's 7-year data set and subsequent follow-up observations. 
We have analyzed the broad emission lines of 15 AGN observed over the 2004-2014 period, and our results show that 8 objects exhibit significant changes in line width, flux, and shift, indicating variations in their emission line regions. 
One object, 0056-0540, displayed a 0.4 eV shift, and we attributed this to a possible gravitational redshift caused by a supermassive black hole with M = 10 billion solar masses. 
We have also found that the broad emission lines of AGN typically change by 0.1-0.3 in flux, with some objects experiencing larger variations. 
Our analysis reveals that the broad emission lines of AGN typically maintain a constant width, although we identified one object, 2005-0440, which exhibited a 1800 km/s width change, suggesting a possible change in the accretion mode. 
Our results show that the broad emission lines of AGN typically maintain a constant shift, although we identified one object, 0056-0540, which exhibited a 0.2 eV shift, suggesting a possible change in the accretion mode.

This analysis delves into the core of Quantum Darwinism providing a streamlined interpretation. It explains how the interaction between a system and its environment results in the emergence of an objective classical reality. By focusing on the information distribution between the system and its environment, it demonstrates that objective reality is formed by the environmental many-body entanglement which then transfers to the system's entanglement with the environment. Utilizing a simplified model, it demonstrates how the information becomes distributed via the entanglement entropy of the environment's correlations. It further shows that this information is made manifest through the entanglement entropy of the system with the environment by employing a partial transpose approach.

This paper explores the properties of the reachable set resulting from applying a sequence of polyhedral approximations of a discrete-time dynamical system's constraints. We analyze the properties of this set by iteratively applying a Minkowski sum of a polyhedron with an ellipsoid, then derive bounds on its convexity, dimension, and the behavior of its level sets under iterative Minkowski sums and section operations.

The SAINT model, a self-attention based neural network, has been found to be highly effective in solving tabular data problems, achieving results comparable to those of traditional machine learning models on specific tasks. However, its performance has yet to be rigorously evaluated on a wide range of benchmark datasets. Our study examines the performance of the SAINT model on 21 established datasets for 7 different problems, and we find that it outperforms standard machine learning models, including decision trees and support vector machines, on most occasions. Our analysis also reveals that the model's performance can be further improved through the use of ensemble methods.

Transfer learning, which enables the utilization of a trained model's knowledge in a new domain with limited data, has been extensively researched in recent years. However, the impact of domain similarity on its effectiveness remains poorly understood. A novel approach called Domain Similarity Measurement (DSM) is proposed to assess the similarity between source and target domains. This method, which is grounded in the concept of cross-domain label distributions, was tested using a range of image datasets and demonstrated a strong correlation with the accuracy of transfer learning. Consequently, it can serve as a reliable indicator for selecting the most suitable source model for transfer learning in a particular domain.

Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) is the most suitable theory for describing the behavior of particles at very small distances. Within this framework, the breakdown of chiral symmetry is a key phenomenon that can be studied by analyzing the behavior of particles in the presence of a specific background. This research focuses on a specific type of background that gives rise to a chiral condensate, which in turn influences the behavior of a state that can be described by a worldsheet that is almost flat. This nearly flat state gives rise to a state that can be described by a string, and by analyzing the behavior of this string in relation to the background, we can determine the behavior of the chiral condensate. This can be done by studying the motion of the string in the background, which in turn allows us to determine the coefficient of the chiral condensate operator. This research also explores the behavior of the string Hamiltonian in the background, which in turn allows us to determine the behavior of the chiral condensate within the background. This research then uses the results obtained to determine the coefficient of the chiral condensate operator, which in turn allows us to make predictions about the behavior of the chiral condensate in the background.

A recent study conducted by the ATLAS Collaboration analyzed Proton-lead collisions to investigate dark matter creation through the process of vector mediator production. This investigation focused on a specific type of mediator, interacting with Standard Model particles via a Higgs-like coupling. Data collected during Run 1, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 3.6 nanobarns in the 5.96 TeV center-of-mass energy range, were utilized in the analysis. Following a comprehensive background evaluation, researchers applied a selection process to the samples, resulting in a final dataset with 20.4 nanoflavoured events. This was found to be consistent with the expected background levels. As a result, researchers established an upper limit of 1.1 pb at a 95% confidence level for dark matter mass of 100 GeV, corresponding to a cross-section of 0.0075 pb in the bb channel. Furthermore, a study of the bphob channel revealed an upper limit of 0.025 pb at a 95% confidence level, indicating that the bb channel is more restrictive. This study's findings are compared with other theoretical models and the results are interpreted in the context of a Higgs-portal model.

Researchers have identified the challenge of determining where a particular concept is located within a software development process as a key issue. To address this, a new approach is proposed that leverages collective knowledge gained from similar software engineering problems encountered by developers. This is achieved by analyzing a large database of developer questions posted on the popular platform Stack Overflow. By applying a tailored clustering technique, the new approach is able to identify the most relevant information related to a software concept and its associated challenges, leading to improved developer problem-solving capabilities. To validate this approach, a prototype tool is developed and tested using developers' problem-solving behavior, and the results show that it is capable of accurately categorizing software concepts and their associated challenges, thereby facilitating more effective developer problem-solving.

This paper develops a block-diagonal preconditioner to efficiently solve complex linear systems emerging from the finite element method. The proposed preconditioner is derived from a new, novel block matrix that can be applied directly to systems with both Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. When used in conjunction with an advanced Krylov subspace method, such as the generalized minimum residual method, the preconditioner significantly reduces computational costs. The proposed preconditioner is demonstrated to be effective through numerical experiments, achieving a remarkable reduction in the number of iterations required to obtain a solution.

In the field of abstractive dialogue summarization, previous research has shown that incorporating discourse relations can be beneficial. However, these relations are often represented in a complex, graph format, making it difficult for neural models to learn from them directly.
