Theoretical findings are complemented by numerical examples illustrating the model's dynamics and optimal control strategies.

The development of next-generation gravitational wave detectors, particularly the third generation, promises significant improvements in binary black hole mergers detection. This is due to their capacity to capture a range of frequencies, including those that will be measurable in the (3,3) and (4,4) modes. This study examines the potential for measuring the (3,3) and (4,4) modes in the aforementioned detectors by simulating binary black hole populations. The results indicate that third-generation detectors will be able to detect approximately 40% of the (3,3) mode and about 20% of the (4,4) mode in binary black hole mergers. The (4,4) mode detection is largely contingent on the detection of the (3,3) mode. The study also found that the (3,3) and (4,4) modes will be more readily measurable in binaries with larger mass ratios and lower masses. The analysis revealed that the (3,3) and (4,4) modes will be less precise in binaries with low masses and higher masses. The study also found that the (3,3) and (4,4) modes will be less precisely determined in binaries with low masses and higher masses.

A new method to identify astrometric binaries containing a black hole has been developed using a combination of astrometric parameters. The proposed model utilizes the radius of curvature and orbital velocity to distinguish between astrometric binaries, with one of them being a compact object, and those consisting of a star and a main sequence companion. The new method was tested using simulated data from the Gaia space telescope, which generated binary populations consistent with observational data. As a result, it was found that the radius of curvature and orbital velocity can effectively distinguish between different binary types, even when the compact object is a black hole. Furthermore, it was discovered that the radial velocity amplitude and orbital period of the binary pair are not reliable indicators of a black hole companion. The proposed method will be used to search for astrometric binaries in real Gaia data, providing valuable insights into the properties of compact objects.

To effectively apply evolutionary algorithms, it's crucial to choose the optimal combination of crossover and selection methods. In this study, we investigated the influence of different crossover and selection methods on a simple 0/1 knapsack problem and found that the best convergence rates are achieved when using uniform crossover with a binary selection method, specifically the (1+1) model.

This research focuses on estimating the L2 norm of a specific integral, Xα.φ(λ0+λ), as λ approaches infinity. Here, φ is a real-valued function that combines a polynomial, P, and a smooth component, f. It is established that if φ is a polynomial, the Xα.φ(λ+λ0) estimates behave similarly to those for the Xα.λm. Furthermore, this result has significant implications for Eguchi's multilinear eigenvalue inequalities, specifically enhancing them with improved constants and broader applicability. On the other hand, when φ is primarily composed of a smooth function, the estimates diverge from those associated with linear phases, leading to novel geometric applications, such as refined estimates for the L2 norm of the vector field ∇u, L2 control of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and a generalized version of the Strichartz inequality in critical Lebesgue spaces.

The automatic detection of hate speech on social media platforms has become increasingly important, and this study focuses on addressing the specific task of identifying hate speech that is offensive to a particular group within the Arabic language. Utilizing a shared dataset of annotated tweets collected from the Arabic microblogging platform, Twitter, this research employed two separate models to analyze the dataset and obtain the highest scores in various categories. In the classification of hate speech that is directed towards a particular group, a model achieved a score of 0.92, while another model performed well in the classification of hate speech that is not targeted at a particular group, with scores of 0.87 and 0.92, respectively. Furthermore, this study also explores the impact of different group labels on the performance of the models, finding that the classification of hate speech that is directed towards women performed better, with scores of 0.90 for the first model and 0.87 for the second model.

Quantum Monte Carlo simulations can efficiently model complex systems with numerous atoms, but they often struggle with computational power demands due to the high computational requirements of these simulations. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed a new approach to reduce the computational complexity of quantum Monte Carlo simulations. This new method involves a new step in the algorithm where the Hamiltonian is separated into distinct parts, which are then treated in separate calculations. These calculations involve the evaluation of forces against atomic positions, which is particularly challenging for systems with high atomic numbers. However, by factoring the Hamiltonian in this way, researchers have found that the computational complexity can be significantly reduced, with the required computational power increasing at a much slower rate with the number of atoms. This new approach has been successfully tested on a range of complex systems, including transition metal oxides, which is a particularly challenging task. This new method has been found to be particularly useful in simulations of systems with high atomic numbers, which is a crucial requirement for accurate modeling of complex systems.

In the 2020 US presidential election, social media platform Twitter restricted access to users who spread false information about voter fraud, generating controversy surrounding censorship and freedom of speech. To better understand the dynamics between Twitter and information control, we analyzed user behavior before and after restrictions were imposed on 1,832 accounts by the platform. Our findings suggest that Twitter's actions led to users spreading misinformation elsewhere, either immediately or after restrictions were put in place, with a 78% increase in such activity 2-4 weeks after the ban. Additionally, users who spread misinformation adapted by utilizing fresh hashtags, with a 50% increase in new hashtag creation immediately after restrictions were put in place. These results indicate that while Twitter's actions may have marginally reduced misinformation on the platform, the overall information spread remains intact, with a significant portion of it happening off-platform.

We establish that for systems exhibiting SRB measures, the Hausdorff dimension of the set of points exhibiting high emergence is directly linked to that same dimension for SRB measure. Additionally, our analysis extends to certain non-mixing scenarios involving partially hyperbolic systems, including surface diffeomorphisms with indifferent fixed points and partially hyperbolic flows.

Deep Bayesian neural networks are known for their ability to quantify uncertainty in output while providing robustness against noisy labels. However, this approach is computationally intensive, necessitating efficient methods to optimize training. This paper presents a novel optimization technique, leveraging variational autoencoders to create a more efficient posterior distribution for DBNNs. The proposed method, demonstrating superior performance on both synthetic and real-world data, offers a more accurate representation of DBNNs' inherent uncertainty. As a result, it can provide more reliable estimates of DBNNs' uncertainty and enhance training efficiency. The approach also offers a way to reduce complexity in large-scale DBNN training.

The theory of instantons offers a wealth of insights into the mechanisms of chemical reactions, which can be particularly valuable when combined with cutting-edge experimental techniques that provide detailed information about these processes. In this article, instanton theory is applied to a specific type of reaction where an electron transfers between two ions in different states of quantum equilibrium, which is influenced by a variable that is measured during the reaction. We derive the key equations needed to calculate the rate of reaction in this context and discuss the experimental methods that could be used to determine the crucial parameters required for this calculation.

This research introduces a control design strategy that integrates model-based control systems with learning-based safety protocols to ensure safe trajectory tracking in robots. The proposed approach addresses the limitations of traditional model-based control under real-world conditions by integrating a data-driven control system to correct for model inaccuracies and ensure overall system safety. The safety module utilizes data-driven control to identify and mitigate errors in the model-based system, utilizing predictive learning to anticipate potential tracking errors and prevent potential issues before they occur. The proposed methodology is comprehensive, enabling simultaneous learning and data utilization for safety applications in both simulation and real-world settings. The approach is applied to the task of safe path following in robots, utilizing data-driven control to identify and mitigate errors in the model-based system, and demonstrating the effectiveness of the method through extensive simulation tests on an open robot system.

The thermoelectric properties of the $T_{C} \approx 11$ K Lanthanum-tungsten-oxygen-xenon alloy system have been investigated using a tungsten-based impurity band model. This model suggests that the tungsten-rich sample primarily exhibits ionic conductivity from the tungsten-based impurity band, while electron hopping between impurity sites contributes to the system's electronic transport. Furthermore, the tungsten-based impurity band is responsible for the thermoelectric properties, which are significantly enhanced by the introduction of xenon.

The perfect sum problem, a classic example illustrated by Knuth [2] as a challenging NP problem, involves finding two numbers within a given range of $x$, which is greater than a certain range $[m]$, that add up to $x$ but are as far apart as possible. The best-known deterministic algorithm to solve this problem has a time complexity of $m$, and Monte Carlo simulations based on random sampling face a similar time complexity. This study proposes a probabilistic solution that uses a fixed amount of time $c \log m$ to find a suboptimal solution with high probability. The solution involves finding the closest pairs with minimal distance to the perfect sum, and we show that the proposed method outperforms the optimal solution with a constant factor of $1 + \epsilon$ for any $\epsilon > 0$.

We suggest an approach to calculating elements of finite fields, which only necessitates knowing the prime factorization of $m$ and a specific set of polynomials $a$. This method yields an iterative process that uses only basic operations and elementary functions, requiring no multiplicative inverses. Furthermore, it can be applied to construct primitive elements of finite fields, provided that the irreducibility of the polynomial $x^m-a$ holds true.

This study introduces a novel strategy synthesis algorithm for parallel software. The algorithm identifies sequences of input data that force the software to reach certain states in its state machine model, taking into account both the software's state transitions and system outputs. By leveraging recent advancements in model checking and the latest state-of-the-art SAT-based algorithm Qsmt, the algorithm effectively targets real-world software with complex states and transitions. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that our algorithm can be modified to synthesize input sequences from arbitrary states to all states in cyclic systems, showcasing its applicability to common types of parallel software. Experimental results confirm the algorithm's effectiveness in synthesizing input sequences for multiple software examples.

Our proposed metasurface imaging system can enhance the resolution of standard optical systems by utilizing spatial frequency filtering. This research presents optimized configurations that offer a two-fold increase in imaging resolution beyond the diffraction limit, leveraging the metasurface's ability to manipulate optical responses. We examine the theoretical underpinnings, experimental limitations, and potential real-world applications, including the recovery of latent images from partially available data. Moreover, this technology can provide robustness against noise in imaging processes.

The population of hydrogen's excited states resulting from a combination of laser fields - consisting of weak, linearly polarized infrared and strong, circularly polarized ultraviolet pulses - applied sequentially, has been studied in response to varying pulse durations and time delays between the pulses. Researchers investigated the effects of this laser combination on the population of states up to the 30th Rydberg state, observing that UV pulses with a 180-degree polarization relative to infrared can significantly reduce population in Rydberg states, especially for short pulse durations. Furthermore, infrared pulses applied for 1.67 ps before the UV pulse can suppress population in Rydberg states, especially for short time delays, allowing for selective population in higher states with the right pulse duration.

This study presents a straightforward yet effective method to enhance semi-supervised learning performance by generating augmented mixed samples from distinct images.  The proposed approach automatically groups similar images based on a predefined feature to create a diverse set of mixed samples.  By incorporating these mixed samples into the training data, the model learns to identify and differentiate between instances of different classes.  Experimental results demonstrate that this method can be integrated seamlessly into various semi-supervised learning frameworks and yields improved results across multiple datasets, including CIFAR-10, Fungi, and Stanford Dogs datasets.

Genes often don't always produce, and when they do, the amount can vary significantly each time, making it difficult to accurately predict the amount of protein produced as a population. In order to gain a deeper understanding of how this occurs, researchers have developed advanced mathematical models that can accurately describe the behavior of large groups of cells, but these models require a significant number of unknown parameters. Fortunately, the same models can also help with optimizing experiments to find the right parameters, and with the help of a specialized optimization method, the results show that the required number of data points is directly related to the number of unknown parameters. In the case of a specific model, the minimum number of data points required grows in proportion to the number of unknown parameters.

In many machine learning applications, graph structures are used to represent relationships or interactions between objects. Developing efficient learning algorithms often relies on adjusting their hyperparameters. This paper introduces a learning approach that allows graph nodes to determine their hyperparameters based on the properties of adjacent nodes, making it more suitable for large sparse graphs. As a result, computational complexity is reduced and system performance can be improved. The proposed method is applied to a real-world problem of designing a decentralized control system for interconnected power grids.

In the field of quantum computing, Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) stands out for its potential to address challenging problems. QAOA combines the strengths of quantum and classical computing, improving the efficiency of difficult optimization problems. The algorithm's performance on various problems has been extensively evaluated. The present research focuses on the impact of errors occurring during dephasing on QAOA's behavior when training with the variational quantum eigensolver's loss function. The study reveals that these errors accelerate the algorithm's convergence but also increase its risk of getting stuck in local optima. The findings are supported by numerical simulations on single and multi-qubit systems. These results provide valuable insights for developing robust QAOA applications.

The field of Person Re-Identification has gained considerable attention due to its numerous practical applications, primarily because it addresses the issue of re-matching individuals across separate camera views, a scenario that occurs in surveillance systems and other related fields.  The current state-of-the-art methods in Person Re-ID typically utilize a two-step process involving feature extraction and comparison.  The extraction of features is usually achieved through the use of convolutional neural networks (CNN) and the use of metric learning techniques for the comparison step.  This paper presents a unified approach that integrates both feature extraction and comparison into a single step, by employing a ResNet architecture, and proposes a new loss function called the Contrastive-Boosting loss function (CB_loss).  The CB_loss function is based on the principle of contrast enhancement and boosting, which aims to reduce the inter-class distance and increase the intra-class distance.  The effectiveness of the CB_loss function is demonstrated by its ability to significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmark datasets, including the MSMT, RMBD-MMAR, RegDB, and DUATTE datasets.

The increasing demand for high-accuracy and high-speed data has driven a growing need for reliable and accurate machine learning algorithms. The creation of vast amounts of data through online services has become a significant obstacle, making it difficult to generate data with specific properties, such as high-fidelity time series data for power systems. To address this issue, this study introduces a new approach using the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) technique, a powerful sampling method, to produce synthetic time series data for power systems that align with historical patterns. The HMC algorithm enables the use of continuous distributions in data generation, and our proposed method, PowerHMC, utilizes the HMC framework to produce time series data for power systems that can be used for training machine learning models. The effectiveness of PowerHMC is evaluated through a series of experiments, and our results show that the generated synthetic data effectively captures the temporal and spatial relationships present in actual power system time series data.

This study focuses on the convergence of iterative processes in the presence of multiple solutions to variational inequality problems. Under specific iteratively adjusted learning and step-size sequences, it is demonstrated that these processes can converge to a common solution when the set of minimal solutions is non-empty and consists of a single element, assuming the underlying function is monotone and Lipschitz continuous. Furthermore, it is shown that these processes can only converge to a minimal solution if the set of minimal solutions is unique.

We provide an overview of several key conjectures concerning the Lyapunov exponents of Folner weights in Fuchsian groups and some specific instances where these conjectures hold true. Notably, we confirm Salpoutzis-Soulis's conjecture for certain notable groups: parabolic, Lorentzian lattices, and the surface group with a single cusp. Additionally, we establish an extension of Kerckhoff-Minsky's theorem to certain non-arithmetic cases and specify the conditions under which this extended theorem holds. Furthermore, we validate a particular instance of the Soul\'s conjecture, relating to the entropy of certain elements in Fuchsian groups.

The ATLAS and CMS collaborations have conducted extensive searches for the $\Upsilon$ quark's decay into a pair of charged Higgs and leptons. These studies were carried out at the LHC, examining proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy, within the 60-110 GeV mass range for the $\Upsilon$ quark. Notably, these searches have been performed for the $\Upsilon$ charge states $\Upsilon^+$ and $\Upsilon^-$, in conjunction with the $\ell$ lepton channels $\ell e ar{
u}_e

Our research involves the structural, electronic, and superconducting characteristics of the compound Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ under high-pressure conditions. By combining density functional theory and density functional theory-based tight-binding parameters, we mapped the electronic band structure, analyzed electronic properties, and determined the superconducting transition temperature. The results show that Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ transforms into a B8 structure above 3.5 GPa, and this change affects its electronic behavior. As pressure increases from 0.5 GPa to 8 GPa, the superconducting transition temperature $T_{\rm C}$ rises from 4.2 K to 5.1 K. The superconducting mechanism in Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ remains consistent and is driven primarily by the electron-phonon interaction.

A new approach to the black hole information paradox is explored through a novel
equation linking an infalling observer's experience at the black hole horizon to
their proper time before being released back out. This relationship, known as
$h=\xi A/h$, where $h$ is proper horizon time, $\xi$ is a dimensionless
factor, and $A$ is the horizon area, is derived from a Dall'Amico-Libassi proposal
involving the study of near-horizon geometry of extremal black holes. The authors
investigate the implications of this equation on the black hole information paradox
and the concept of firewalls, concluding that a smooth recovery of quantum states
is achievable at the horizon, along with the preservation of information. The
authors also discuss potential experimental verification of the proposed solution.

Neural ODEs have gained popularity in modeling vector fields, but their ability to accurately capture dynamics from noisy measurements remains uncertain due to difficulties in interpreting and refining their results. To address this, we have developed a novel framework that optimizes model parameters to align with the underlying dynamics of a system. By leveraging this framework, we can derive reliable vector field approximations from noisy data and make meaningful inferences about the model parameters. This optimization process is facilitated through an adjoint method, requiring the solution of two ordinary differential equations, one forward and one backward in time. The approach has been successfully applied to a mathematical model of the CaSPR network, a biological pathway regulating cellular responses to extracellular signals.

We introduce the Object Memory Transformer (OMT), a navigation model that
employs a spatially informed attention mechanism to extract relevant information
from object-based landmarks in 3D environments. By leveraging object features
and a novel memory augmentation technique, OMT significantly enhances the
efficiency of navigation in complex indoor spaces. Experimental evaluations on
the Replica-Benchmark and RoomNet datasets reveal OMT's superiority over existing
state-of-the-art methods by achieving a notable 60% reduction in trajectory
length and a 40% decrease in interaction costs while maintaining equivalent
success rates for long-term navigation.

This study examines the instruction-tuning process for large language models, a method that modifies pre-trained models to perform various tasks efficiently. By applying a theoretical framework, we investigate how the size, structure, and fine-tuning data affect the performance of these models, both in terms of general capabilities and task-specific skills. Our analysis reveals that increasing model size leads to improved performance, largely due to an increase in model capacity. Additionally, we identified a critical role for fine-tuning data in developing task-specific representations within the model. Finally, we observed that the models exhibit a hierarchical structure, where task-specific representations are built upon more general capabilities.

Informal online groups that share a common interest tend to be valuable learning resources, offering members the opportunity to engage in 'legitimate peripheral learning.' In these collaborative environments, participants can acquire foundational and advanced skills, as well as explore new topics, benefitting even experienced professionals. This informal 'community-driven learning' model is being examined through a multi-faceted study that focuses on the learning processes within these groups. The study consists of three main components: Firstly, a survey was conducted to identify the common characteristics and features of these learning communities. Secondly, a 'legitimate peripheral participation' model was developed to illustrate the learning journey of individuals within these groups. Lastly, a set of design patterns were proposed to facilitate community-driven learning. The study's preliminary findings are promising and warrant further investigation and validation.

The transcorrelated method, inspired by Cullen's approach, is evaluated for treating complex many-body problems in real spaces. A modified version of this approach is implemented, where a specific weight function is used to achieve a more accurate description of metallic systems. This approach is demonstrated to be effective in describing metallic systems by comparing it with the random phase approximation, and it is further shown to be an extension of the standard transcorrelated method. The modified transcorrelated method is also compared with other approximations, including the local density approximation, and it is found to be an improvement over these methods. The accuracy of the transcorrelated method is also verified through its ability to reproduce the exchange correlation energy in a defect-free system, and it is found to be in good agreement with the density functional theory results.

A mathematical framework is developed to address the issue of unknown location, allowing a small variation in the location of a quantity to be systematically integrated into a deterministic system. The method maintains the conservation of physical properties such as mass and energy. The framework is applied to study advection in a 1D system with variable velocity, using a 2nd order finite volume discretization. The results show that our approach yields a consistent and convergent numerical method. The accuracy of the new scheme is demonstrated by comparing it with a reference solution obtained from an advection-invertible transport equation. The method is further validated through various numerical tests.

A theoretical framework, rooted in information theory, has been proposed to address the complex issues of big data storage and processing. This framework integrates randomness and entropy principles to optimize data distribution and utilization across various nodes, thereby enhancing overall computational efficiency. Key concepts of the framework enable the simultaneous management of multiple data sets, prioritizing their priority levels, and establishing an accurate prediction model. As a foundational component, a novel device mapping algorithm employs randomness and entropy to partition and allocate data among nodes, ensuring efficient device management. Empirical evaluations using both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the validity and performance of the framework, particularly its ability to accelerate computation by upscaling the number of nodes.

To ensure that autonomous robots can adapt seamlessly to real-world environments using pre-trained policies, we propose the Safe Adaptive Policy Transfer (SafeAPT) approach. It enables a pre-trained policy in a simulated environment to directly apply to a real-world setting with minimal risk of encountering unforeseen situations. Our method leverages a set of constraints learned from the simulated environment, which are then enforced on real-world trajectories. However, this may cause the agent to become stagnant due to the risk of neglecting novel states. To mitigate this, our algorithm monitors and updates an approximation of novel states, effectively navigating unknown situations while maintaining safety. Through comprehensive experiments on both simulated and real robots, we demonstrate the efficacy of SafeAPT in efficiently exploring new environments while maintaining safety.

The Fanaroff-Riley (FR) classification system categorizes radio galaxies into two types based on their morphologies: FR I and FR II. This classification system has been extensively used for many years, but its application has been hindered by the difficulty of obtaining accurate images of galaxies at z>5. This has led to a lack of a comprehensive understanding of the evolution of radio structures in these galaxies. A recent study has provided a comprehensive view of the FR classification system by analyzing a sample of 143 radio galaxies at z<1.1. The study found that the FR classification scheme is primarily a morphological classification, with the shape of the radio structure being the key factor in distinguishing between FR I and FR II sources. Additionally, the study found that the ratio of the radio structure's length to its width is a key factor in distinguishing between the two types of sources. The study also investigated the relationship between the central black hole and radio structure, and found that the FR classification system is related to the mass of the central black hole. This suggests that the central black hole plays a crucial role in shaping the radio structure, with more massive black holes producing longer FR II sources. The study also found that the FR II sources are more likely to be found in high-density environments, such as in the centers of galaxy clusters. This suggests that the central black holes in these sources are able to feed and produce powerful radio jets, which are then quenched by the surrounding hot intracluster medium.

We address the issue of testing whether real-valued functions align with the pattern predicted by a known function of real variables. Unlike existing procedures that rely on specific assumptions about the functions being tested, our proposed method is more universal and compatible with functions of any form. The testing procedure developed in this research is fully data-driven and doesn't require any pre-existing knowledge about the functions being tested. The approach is tested on functions of polynomial and exponential forms and demonstrates its reliability. The research also explores the sensitivity of data-driven testing procedures to the distribution of data, finding that the performance of our proposed method is largely unaffected by the distribution of data, except in the most extreme cases. The analysis reveals that the only factor that significantly influences the performance of our proposed method is the amount of data available.

This study introduces a dataset of 221k human-rated tweets concerning 50 medical conditions, leveraging expert evaluations to establish accurate references. We introduce a novel benchmark for using AI models to assist healthcare professionals in categorizing social media content. We assess the effectiveness of various models in a binary framework, finding that multilingual models outperform monolingual models, with a particularly significant improvement seen in resource-constrained languages. The research also explores the impact of model size and training signals on accuracy, highlighting a trade-off between these factors.

A novel approach for diagnosing distinct brain disorders using neuroimaging data
in individuals of various ages is proposed. It integrates a deep learning framework
with a hierarchical model for extracting informative functional MRI data features
from both local brain regions and full brain scans. The method's effectiveness is
evaluated using a combined dataset of Alzheimer's disease patients and healthy
controls from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, which was collected
in multiple age groups. We employed convolutional neural networks to identify key
features in both local brain regions and full brain scans, then combined them to
classify the brain disorders. The classification results demonstrate that our
method outperforms conventional approaches, such as the Monte Carlo method, which
simulates a realistic clinical environment. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that
the brain regions most crucial for diagnosis vary significantly between healthy
individuals and those with Alzheimer's disease, depending on the age of the subject.

This paper investigates the control of a one-dimensional nonhomogeneous Euler equation and establishes the well-posedness of a related optimal control problem. The system is defined within a bounded domain and involves nonlinear energy loss. We analyze the impact of this loss on the control system's convergence rate and show that it significantly influences the exponential stability of the system. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the reduced-order model's accuracy and validate the convergence of the reduced-order model through numerical simulations.

A novel method for handling domain boundaries in high-order numerical schemes has been developed using a approach inspired by flux reconstruction. This approach involves upwinding high-order numerical schemes at the boundary to enhance stability, accuracy, and mesh flexibility. The proposed boundary treatment method was successfully applied to the discontinuous Galerkin (DG) and flux reconstruction (FR) methods, and numerical experiments demonstrated its efficacy. Notably, the method was shown to recover the expected theoretical order of convergence for a wide range of numerical problems.

Our study examines how the thickness of a silicon film in a photonic crystal layer affects its optical absorption and emission when illuminated by a laser. The silicon film is placed between two times five times photonic crystal mirrors, creating a resonant optical cavity with a cavity length of 2.7 micrometers. The results show that increasing the silicon film thickness from 30 nanometers to 240 nanometers results in enhanced absorption and emission. The absorption rate reaches 100% at thick silicon films, while the maximum emission peak occurs in the wavelength range around 1550 nanometers. The peak wavelength can be adjusted by varying the crystal's lattice constant, allowing it to be tuned from 1475 nanometers to 1250 nanometers when the lattice constant is changed from 500 nanometers to 625 nanometers. The observed emission peak is attributed to the Purcell effect within the photonic crystal environment.

This paper provides an in-depth look at the credal sets, which offer a geometric interpretation of sets of valuations, and are studied from a theoretical and algorithmic perspective. Key operations like union, intersection, and complement have been explicitly defined. We present a direct approach to calculate fixed points of operations involving credal sets, which is then applied to analyze convex sets and min-max valuations. We establish the existence and uniqueness of fixed points for credal sets, which is a critical aspect in the credal set program. Furthermore, we propose an efficient computational strategy for credal set operations and demonstrate its application in solving linear programming problems through credal set operations.

We suggest a distance-driven recommendation model that uses a distance metric to match test users with items from the training data set. The proposed model calculates the distance between users and items, then identifies the item most similar to the user, using either the minimum or maximum distance metric as chosen. The distance is measured as the $W_2$ distance between the user and item distributions, represented by their learned embeddings. We demonstrate the model's ability to effectively process both continuous and categorical data, showcasing its efficacy through a series of experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets.

We explore the quantum capacity of a class of qutrit channels known as the quasi-energy qutrit Gorini, Albert, Karassioi, Plenio (GAD) channel. This channel acts as a two-way communication system, and its behavior is governed by an eternally non-Markovian property, $E(t)$. Our research shows that the GAD channel's capacity can be described using a set of parameters that depend on the energy parameter, $t$, due to the channel's non-Markovian nature. Our results also reveal that the GAD channel's capacity can be expressed in terms of the energy parameter, $t$, which is a characteristic of the channel's energy-dependent behavior.

In many real-world applications, the training and testing datasets are from different sources. Therefore, it's crucial to evaluate a model's ability to generalize to unseen data across multiple domains. To address this issue, we've developed a new approach called CCRAL (Conditional Conditional Independence Ratio) to quantify the complexity of a model based on its domains. Our CCRAL method calculates the model's complexity by evaluating how independent its predictions are across different domains, providing a fair comparison of models across various datasets. To improve model generalization, we've also developed a novel domain-adaptive transfer learning approach, leveraging our CCRAL method to select the optimal weights for model ensembles. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing model ensemble techniques, particularly when training and testing datasets come from different sources.

The semantic mapping process involves merging a topological map of locations
with attribute data such as object locations, like tables or chairs, which
represents a crucial component in many robotic systems.  Despite its
importance, semantic mapping poses significant challenges, including the
need to constantly update topological segments and attribute data in real
time while also considering the potential negative impact on the map
structure when detecting and removing attributes.  In our work, we introduce a
novel framework that utilizes a structured generative model to efficiently
update topological and attribute data in real-time while minimizing map
distortion.  We validate the performance of our framework through extensive
simulations using the widely recognized HERB 2 simulator.

The Rikudo puzzle is a variant of the Slitherlink puzzle that we reframe as a graph partitioning problem. By considering a graph where each number represents a node, and edge capacities reflect constraints from the grid, we can solve this graph within a polynomial time frame. Specifically, we can identify an optimal solution in polynomial time when all odd numbers are placed on either the same or dissimilar parallel lines.

The Sinkhorn's algorithm is a crucial tool for efficiently solving optimization problems in machine learning, such as approximating Wasserstein distances and transport equations, due to its reliance on Bregman divergences. However, its application in high-dimensional scenarios is hindered by the complexity of solving non-convex optimization problems. This paper presents a novel, first-order method for optimizing Bregman divergences with a simple, separable structure, and demonstrates its ability to solve Sinkhorn's problem in high dimensions. Additionally, the method's application in solving other optimization problems arising from Bregman divergences is explored, with a focus on its use in generating sparse solutions through additional constraints.

Given a reciprocal integer sequence defined by its periodicity and parity, represented by a set of matrices $(A_0, A_1, \ldots, A_{p-1})$, the properties of the matrices can be analyzed to derive the properties of the solutions to the generalized modular equation and a polynomial equation $P(\varphi, \varphi) = 0$, specifically the Hecke matrix $M_t$. Additionally, the solutions can be expressed as roots of a quartic equation in $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_4)$ and the discriminant of the polynomial $P(\varphi, \varphi)$ is connected to the discriminants of the quadratic and the quartic polynomials.

We have conducted a thorough examination of two galaxy lens systems, J0818-2613 and J1817+293, utilizing the Hubble Space Telescope.  The observations of J0818-2613 were taken with the WFC3 G141 and G280 filters, while for J1817+293 we used the WFC3 G141 and the Wide Field Camera 3's infrared capabilities.  The data collected on J0818-2613 has enabled us to obtain a highly accurate redshift measurement of 1.697 for the primary lensing object, as well as a determination of the magnification of the central deflector.  The observations of J1817+293 have yielded a redshift of 2.295 for the main deflecting group, as well as a more precise estimate of the redshift of 0.833 for the secondary lensing object.  The data collected on J1818-2613 has enabled us to obtain a highly accurate estimate of the lens's mass profile, while the data collected on J1817+293 has enabled us to obtain a highly accurate estimate of the lens's mass profile, as well as a highly accurate estimate of the lens's mass profile, as well as a highly accurate estimate of the lens's mass profile, as well as a highly accurate estimate of the lens's mass profile, as well as a highly accurate estimate of the lens's mass profile, as well as a highly accurate estimate of the lens's

This research presents an innovative approach to solving a $q$-fractional differential equation with constant coefficients, where the initial values are given for the first time. By utilizing the $q$-fractional integral operator, we rephrase the problem and then develop a numerical solution using the difference method. Our method involves constructing a $q$-difference equation, whose coefficients are determined by the constant coefficients of the $q$-fractional differential equation, and whose right-hand side is expressed as a function of $q$. We provide a concrete example to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed difference method.

The introduction of a magnetic field in dielectric materials yields a non-zero phonon Hall conductivity, which can be measured using the thermoelectric coefficient $\alpha^\star$. This research explores the thermodynamic Hall coefficient at low temperatures in the presence of a magnetic field, in the weak coupling limit of the Universal Optomechanical Coupling (UOMC) material platform. The study reveals that phonon Hall conductivity depends on magnetic field strength and is highly sensitive to material properties, including mass, lattice size and dielectric constant. Our findings demonstrate that phonon Hall conductivity exhibits a linear relationship with magnetic field strength, in accordance with the weak coupling UOMC material.

A novel nod and shuffle technique for wide-field imaging has been developed, allowing the acquisition of a full sky map in a single exposure. By shifting a lens assembly within the instrument's optics and alternating north and south nods, this setup enables the collection of data from a fully overlapping area. This design minimizes acquisition time in wide-field imagers and is particularly beneficial for survey instruments. A functional prototype of the concept has been created and modeled using a computer-aided design software for further analysis and optimization of its design.

A novel and efficient approach to several fundamental inequalities of Choong-Tao Yang has been discovered, offering an alternative perspective that can be seen as a matrix version of the inequalities. This new perspective reveals the utility in using the spectral mapping theorem to establish the efficiency of the inequalities. Building on this, a new set of matrix-based Choong-Tao Yang inequalities has been developed, with the added benefit of being easier to prove. This new method not only provides insight into the original inequalities but also enables the creation of several novel matrix inequalities.

We examine the thermodynamic properties of an evaporating spherically symmetric black hole in the context of the Unruh-deWitt point particle, focusing on the role of the averaged null energy condition in its thermodynamics. Our investigation reveals that this condition is violated as the black hole is formed, and its degree of violation is constant over time. Additionally, the black hole appears to exhibit a temperature decrease in a range of energy levels, and its internal entropy may be increasing, all of which are consistent with the second law of thermodynamics as formulated by Cohen, Kirklin, and Teitelboim.

A four-dimensional Conformal Field Theory with a marginal current operator and a irrelevant operator of integer-conformal-dimension one, is used to model a magnetic field. We investigate the impact of the irrelevant operator on the conformal and chiral anomalies. It is discovered that the irrelevant operator eliminates the chiral anomaly but enhances the trace anomaly. The relevant operator disrupts parity and time-reversal symmetry. We derive the Wess-Zumino-Wilczek term using the instanton method and show that it is unaffected by the irrelevant operator. Our findings are consistent with anomalies obtained using other methods and demonstrate compatibility with the irrelevant operator's influence on the trace anomaly.

The cybersecurity community has developed several Information Systems testbeds to test and assess interdependent systems security. These networks typically comprise various industrial control and information technology components and offer open testing and research opportunities. Most existing testbeds share a common goal: to advance the understanding of industrial control systems and their security. Despite their shared purpose, each has its own set of technologies and resources that are unique and often limited. Existing literature lacks a unified framework for evaluating these differences and the effectiveness of these testbeds in achieving their objectives. This study aims to address this gap by developing a new metric for evaluating testbed maturity and proposing a comprehensive evaluation framework. We also conducted a survey of existing testbeds and evaluated them using our proposed framework. Our results provide valuable insights into the current state of these networks and their potential for future development.

In this research, we present a novel architecture called the Greedy-based Value Representation (GVR). GVR integrates a greedy policy with a value function estimation model, enabling it to learn optimal policies in complex, large-scale Markov Games with limited data. The integration of greedy information enhances the representation's ability to focus on crucial state features, leading to improved performance in multi-agent tasks. The empirical results demonstrate that GVR outperforms other models by a margin of 60% in most scenarios. The successful integration of greedy policies in GVR contrasts with previous research, such as MARL-Nash, which found that Nash equilibrium did not enhance learning in the context of MARL. We anticipate that GVR will inspire further investigation into the utility of greedy-based methods in deep learning applications.

We present StereoSet, a large-scale, open-source dataset designed to assess
stereotypical biases in language models. This comprehensive resource comprises 20,000
human-verified items across four key domains: appearance, lifestyle, personality,
and innate traits. Our analysis reveals that current state-of-the-art language models
exhibit similar stereotypical biases as human subjects, highlighting the need for
further research to create more inclusive AI technologies. This work also outlines initial
strategies for mitigating stereotypical biases and provides StereoSet as a reference
point for future research to evaluate the effectiveness of various methods.

In this paper, we develop a new approach to optimize network resource allocation, where we combine machine learning and decision-making to learn and control tilt update policies in a Contextual Multi-Armed-Bandit framework. This approach allows us to dynamically adjust update policies based on network performance, reducing the need for extensive simulations. By using a novel index to estimate long-term network utility from simulations and integrating learning with decentralized utility optimization, we can achieve efficient and adaptive tilt policies. We validate our model through experiments on a real-world network and show significant improvements over traditional methods.

The $CP$-violating phase gamma, represented by the angle gamma, is determined from a combination of $B$ meson decays. Using data from $772$ fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions collected by the LHCb in 2014 and 2015, the decay rates of the penguin-rich modes $B^+ \to K^+ \pi^0$, $B^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^0$, and $B_s^0 \to \phi \pi^0$ are analyzed. A sample of $B_s^0 \to J/\psi K^+ $ decays is used for calibration purposes. The calculated value of gamma, based on the measured decay rates, is $\gamma = (328.7^{+6.0+6.0}_{-6.6-5.3})^\circ$, where the errors represent the statistical and systematic uncertainties. The combined result has a 95.5% confidence level interval between 1.0 and 34.5 degrees and the 95.0% confidence level interval between 0.2 and 34.7 degrees.

Our research demonstrates a direct relationship between a convex shape's complex symmetry and key properties when considering two-dimensional cross-sections and projections. This finding extends existing knowledge on the relationship between symmetry in higher dimensions and symmetry in projected plans. Notably, we apply our findings to examine and strengthen certain estimates made by K. Boros and B. Bollobás in their study on tetrachromatic circles.

The collection and exchange of personal data has become a widespread practice, and individuals are increasingly active in managing their privacy. This includes actively deciding on the personal data rights they wish to sell or retain. However, the existing market paradigms do not accurately reflect the complex negotiations over data, privacy, and profits. Consequently, the conventional economic models of data trading do not capture the true nature of these transactions as evaluated by laypeople. This study aims to bridge this gap by examining the perceptions of data transactions through a qualitative analysis of people's opinions and ratings of data trading scenarios. The results reveal that laypeople view data trading as a market-driven activity but also recognize the need for non-market elements in regulating data trading. Moreover, the public holds a utilitarian view of data trading that contradicts the prevailing market paradigms. The findings also highlight the need for new data trading paradigms that prioritize public interests and profits.

FTN signaling simplifies detection complexity but introduces increased channel estimation complexity due to its piecewise linear nature. A proposed deep learning solution estimates the channel's piecewise linear coefficients directly from received symbols, outperforming traditional methods when recurrent neural networks are used with autoregressive predictors.

We have derived the 1-dimensional compactification of a Stonean effect algebra with specific properties, building upon a similar construction for distributive lattices. This result, combined with the idea of fundamental effect algebras, allows us to extend this concept to effect algebras. Furthermore, we've established a link between the topologies proposed by Rie\v{c}ak and Zelina for complete effect algebras with a total order, showing that they are equivalent in certain cases, including complete atomic distributive effect algebras. The equivalence of these topologies also depends on whether the effect algebra is finite or countable.

This study delves into the influence of diverse data on the accuracy of object detection models, revealing a notable disparity in performance between models trained on data with uniform characteristics and those trained on data with varied properties. To address this, we introduce SaliencyMix, a novel data augmentation technique that enhances data diversity by combining saliency maps from different models and perspectives. By leveraging SaliencyMix, we found that models trained on augmented data exhibit improved performance in object detection tasks, particularly when using pre-trained models or limited training data. We also observe a significant improvement in model behavior heterogeneity, resulting in reduced false positive rates. The project's code is available at https://github.com/ChangXueHe/SaliencyMix.

Vershik and Kerov made a significant discovery in 1988 by classifying the types of indecomposable positive traces in infinite-dimensional Iwahori-Hecke algebras, achieving a notable outcome that many mathematicians sought. However, it appears the key proof is missing and consideration of the infinite-dimensional scenario with its distinct parameters, along with parameters for the negative and zero cases, was thought to require a complete unitary approach. This paper successfully provides a unifying proof for all instances, including a novel and straightforward method for the negative case.

We have developed a novel approach to assess the effectiveness of the Alcock-Paczynski method using the alignment of shapes and orientations of galaxy clusters at a specific redshift. This method involves analyzing the alignment of galaxy clusters within a particular region, defined by the alignment parameter which represents the correlation between the major axis of a galaxy cluster and the line of sight. This parameter is found to be highly dependent on the redshift and cluster richness. By applying this approach to the Dark Energy Survey's galaxy clusters, we have been able to constrain the alignment parameter and, in turn, the value of $\Omega_{\rm m}(z)$. Our results show that the alignment parameter is consistent with the $\Lambda$CDM cosmology and enable us to constrain $\Omega_{\rm m}(z)$ to a precision of 0.06. This method can be further improved by increasing the number of clusters and implementing more sophisticated statistical tests.

Soft-mechanical models with numerous applications are developed to understand particle systems exhibiting complex stress responses. By applying time-reversal protocols to a specific two-dimensional soft-matter system, we demonstrate that its behavior is non-reversible and retains information about past states. This non-reversibility and retained memory are associated with topological changes in its structure, specifically the formation of entangled networks between particles. Our research shows that a specific topological transition is responsible for the system's non-reversible and memory-exhibiting behavior, and we explore the implications of this phenomenon under controlled experimental conditions.

The phase transition of small gold particles in vacuum from solid to liquid was studied using molecular dynamics simulations. The size of the particles, ranging from 102 to 204 atoms, was examined over 10 ns simulations, revealing a temperature-dependent behavior. It was discovered that smaller particles have a higher melting point than larger particles. Furthermore, the system's equilibrium properties were influenced by thermal fluctuations, resulting in the formation of liquid droplets and solid clusters within the particle.

Reexamining certain classical theories of quasi-linear elliptical boundary value problems, specifically regarding weak solutions, leads to an exploration of their role in the theory of hyperbolic partial differential equations, where a less stringent condition on the differentiability of the quasi-linear operator is considered.

We present a comprehensive model that addresses the Z to tt, uu, mu, nu, tau, anti-mu, anti-tau, anti-tau anomalies by utilizing two new scalar fields, one with a charge of -1/3 and the other with a charge of -1/1, in the presence of a 27-plet Higgs field. The scenario is characterized by a non-standard Higgsino and singlinos that generate quarks and anti-leptons at different energy levels, resulting in a linear relationship between the two. This model predicts a range of new phenomena, including additional Higgs bosons, new fermions, and a 27-plet Higgs field, in addition to a large number of new scalar fields, at the TeV scale. The proposed model predicts a significant number of new production processes, such as the production of the new Higgsinos and singlinos, as well as the production of the new fermions and Higgsinos, in various collision processes, including the production of the new Higgsinos and singlinos, the production of the new fermions and Higgsinos, and the production of the new Higgsinos and Higgsinos, in various collision processes, including the production of the new Higgsinos and singlinos, the production of the new fermions and Higgsinos, and the production of the new Higgsinos and Higgsinos, in various collision processes, indicating a significant potential for

This paper's primary goal is to derive identities involving the (h; q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials with specific weights, utilizing the q-umbral method and its associated algebra. By employing this approach, we can obtain identities related to the (h; q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials that are analogous to well-known identities featuring the Wilson polynomials.

This study focuses on the non-stationary average reward reinforcement learning issue. 
The challenge involves a series of actions leading to unknown reward estimations being calculated at each step. 
The goal is to find the optimal policy that maximizes the average reward over time. 
The approach in this work is to model the non-stationary reward function using a time-varying regression parameter. 
The parameters are estimated via a specific data sampling method involving the optimal policy derived from the previous step. 
The policy obtained using the estimated parameters is then shown to converge to the optimal non-stationary policy under certain conditions. 
Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed algorithm's regret grows logarithmically with time, thus offering an optimal solution to the non-stationary average reward reinforcement learning problem.

This study presents a collection of causal inference tools grounded in the causal odds ratio framework, specifically designed for evaluating treatment effects. These tools facilitate the examination of treatment effects across various dimensions, including the impact of auxiliary variables and multiple treatment scenarios. The COR-based approach offers several key advantages, including the ability to accurately estimate total causal effects, the incorporation of covariates in models, and the capability to assess interaction effects between auxiliary variables and treatments. The proposed methods are applied to a randomized controlled trial dataset to illustrate their utility in real-world applications.

A novel autoencoder design has been proposed, incorporating invertible layers, for generating high-quality samples from high-dimensional, nonlinear, and stochastic processes. By leveraging the natural probability distributions embedded within these systems, the autoencoder learns to replicate these underlying patterns, rather than relying on manually defined and often inaccurate priors. The proposed architecture features a flexible and unsupervised learning framework, utilizing a tailored training objective and the gradient flow of log-likelihood. The experimental findings demonstrate that invertible layer autoencoders deliver superior log-likelihood and sample quality compared to conventional methods, particularly when working with limited data.

This paper outlines the creation and implementation of Thessaland, a multi-dimensional data visualization system with a focus on analyzing smart city data. The system's front-end is easily embeddable within web applications, enabling users to incorporate interactive visualizations. The back-end of Thessaland, powered by a microservices architecture, ensures modularity and efficiency. Developed within the framework of the H2020 SmartCitySOS project, Thessaland evaluates the H2020 Smart City GVC initiative. The paper discusses Thessaland's design, implementation, and evaluation, as well as its potential real-world applications.

In this study, we develop an optimal geometric multigrid preconditioner tailored to hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin methods by leveraging the local characteristics of these finite elements. Our approach is grounded in the fact that the discrete vector space can be divided into distinct subspaces, which are interconnected through a transfer operator. By examining the properties of this operator, we can determine the optimal basis for coarse-scale multigrid methods by selecting the subspaces with the greatest contribution to the underlying linear system. This choice is further optimized by identifying and prioritizing the subspaces with the highest approximation error, resulting in improved efficiency and scalability. Our method is particularly beneficial for handling complex three-dimensional problems, achieving a nearly linear scaling in the number of degrees of freedom. We also investigate the effect of various polynomial degrees and mesh resolutions on the method's performance, which is evaluated using a range of numerical examples.

We introduce a probabilistic approach to identify causal effects from incomplete datasets, leveraging the E-value to validate the reliability of such inferences across various scenarios. By calculating the probability of observing the data given the model assumptions, missing data patterns, and potential alternative explanations, the E-value quantifies the likelihood of the inferred causal effects. We demonstrate how the E-value can be computed under different null hypotheses using the Bayesian bootstrap technique. Furthermore, we provide a general framework to derive E-values for any set of data, identified, and control groups. We also illustrate the application of the E-value framework in three case studies, including a study on the impact of a four-day week on employee productivity, a study examining the effect of a meningococcal conjugate vaccine on bacterial meningitis incidence, and a study assessing the effect of a breast cancer screening program on breast cancer incidence. The results show that the E-values indicate that the inferred causal effects are extremely unlikely to occur by chance, suggesting that the inferences are highly reliable.

In crossover studies with multiple periods and limited participant numbers, handling missing data poses significant challenges. This is because certain individual participant data may coincide with unique time points in only one group, which is often referred to as exchangeable data. This can cause standard statistical methods to be compromised if not properly accounted for. To address this issue, researchers have proposed a Bayesian statistical approach that considers missing data exchangeable and approximates it as White Noise. However, a recent study has shown that assuming data follows a Markov-Gaussian process yields better results and more accurate variance estimates. This paper provides an in-depth explanation of the proposed statistical methodology, presents the derived algorithms, and showcases its effectiveness through a simulation study. Furthermore, we apply this method to an actual clinical trial to obtain a more precise estimate of the treatment effect.

The category's nerve, derived from a given category, is given a topological form. Under a particular set of conditions, it is proven that the topological structure of its nerve is connected to the presence of A_n structures within its category. In the context of categories related to operads, it is shown that the topological form of a category's nerve is equivalent to the homotopy type of the reduced nerve. The concepts developed are applied to study simplicial objects and their properties, and they are specifically used to determine when a simplicial object forms an A_infty structure.

Unpredictable outputs from DRAM unclonable functions (PUFs) based on on-chip voltage countermeasures pose significant challenges in ensuring secure authentication. To address this limitation, our research introduces a novel DRAM PUF that leverages the inherent delay between DRAM cells of different ranks to generate unique identifiers. This innovative approach overcomes the thermal and power constraints faced by previous methods, resulting in a highly reliable DRAM PUF that is resistant to cloning attempts, scalable, and less vulnerable to temperature fluctuations and power cycling. As a result, our proposed system offers superior resilience, higher output reliability, and greater resilience to temperature variations and power cycles, significantly outperforming existing DRAM PUFs in terms of security, scalability, and durability.

As cloud computing continues to evolve, managing virtualized network resources has become increasingly crucial for efficient service delivery. Functional programming, with its inherent benefits, is expected to play a vital role in this evolving landscape. Python, with its vast ecosystem and prominent usage, is likely to contribute significantly to designing programming languages for cloud computing. This article delves into the integration of functional programming, specifically using Python, within the context of cloud computing, virtualized network resources, and managed networked systems.

We utilize the toric code to create a method for continuously assessing the performance of quantum gates at the surface code level. This method employs a reliable standard of accuracy derived from repeated measurements of the toric code's global error rate in a steady state. The developed protocol is capable of providing real-time error estimations for stabilizer circuits, making it suitable for large-scale tasks such as optimizing quantum gate calibration procedures. Numerical simulations indicate that this approach can accurately detect even small percentages of faulty gates present in large quantum circuits.

The increasing adoption of cloud computing and data science workloads across the globe has significantly transformed the IT landscape, resulting in a surge in demand for high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. To address this growing need, researchers have developed a range of innovative solutions, including AutoBayesHops, a framework that leverages a multi-cloud environment to automate HPC job execution. By employing a sophisticated auto-scaling mechanism based on machine learning and a novel job routing algorithm, AutoBayesHops optimizes job placement and execution, while simultaneously reducing costs. We have also extended this framework to integrate a federated blockchain system, focusing on ensuring the security and integrity of job execution. Through comprehensive testing on real-world HCP workloads, we have demonstrated the efficacy of our solution in improving throughput, reducing completion times, and minimizing costs.

The wireless communications and networks community has recently witnessed a surge in interest towards blockchain technology. Researchers are now faced with the daunting task of navigating the complex landscape of blockchain applications, given the sheer volume of emerging solutions. This survey paper aims to provide a structured overview of the applications of blockchain technology in learning wireless communications and networking systems. We begin with a detailed examination of the underlying technologies involved in wireless systems and learning methodologies. Subsequently, we discuss the applications and challenges associated with integrating blockchain technology into wireless systems and learning approaches. Finally, we present a comprehensive outlook for future research directions in this rapidly evolving field.

The discovery of exoplanets with short orbital periods near their host stars has made it possible to study their atmospheres in detail, but the uncertainty in stellar temperatures based on limited data poses a challenge in interpreting the results. To address this issue, we have conducted a series of experiments using a 1D climate model to examine how variations in stellar temperature affect the atmospheric composition and transmission spectra of a planet orbiting a star with a metallicity similar to the Sun. Our findings show that a 10K change in stellar temperature can lead to differences of up to 0.5 in the O2-O3 relationship, and variations in CH3Cl abundance can have a similar impact on the CH4-CH3C2-H2O relationship, depending on the surface temperature and atmospheric pressure. We also found that an overestimation of stellar temperature by 10% can result in an underestimation of H2O abundance by up to 0.3 and an overestimation of CH3C2H2O abundance by up to 0.3. Conversely, an underestimation of stellar temperature by the same percentage can result in an overestimation of H2O abundance by up to 0.3 and an underestimation of CH3C2H2O abundance by up 0.3. Our study highlights the importance of using robust stellar temperature estimates to interpret the atmospheric composition and understand the formation and evolution of exoplanets.

We investigate the phenomenon of surface currents in a one-dimensional system with attractive interactions between bosons and repulsive interactions between any additional fermions. We demonstrate that the surface currents remain stable in both a bosonic system with a positive chemical potential and a fermionic system with any chemical potential. The system's behavior is analyzed through the Bethe ansatz approach, and the results are verified by exact diagonalization. We then examine the influence of the chemical potential on the root distribution, a quantity that can be measured in experiments. We also discuss the implications of our findings in the context of the Fermi-Hubbard model and their potential experimental application in observing fermionic superfluids.

Our research introduces a multilingual neural machine translation model specifically
adapted to the medical domain. This domain-adapted model performs better in medical
translation than a standard model, highlighting the need for specialized translation
models in specific fields. We assess the domain-adapted model's capabilities by
translating new medical texts written in a different style than the original training
data and find that it outperforms a standard model on unseen data. Additionally, we
evaluate the translation of complex medical terms and notes, where domain adaptation
significantly improves accuracy.

This study explores the effects of a ion fluid temperature on the formation of solitary and shock waves within two-dimensional unmagnetized dusty plasmas, where a two-temperature dust grain fluid model is employed. The interaction between the ion fluid temperature and electron nonthermal parameters significantly influence the type of wave formed, with both KdV and modified KdV equations being relevant. The ion fluid temperature and electron nonthermal parameter also dictate the amplitude of shock waves within the dusty plasma system.

This study introduces a contrastive context prediction (CCP) task to improve sentence representations in diverse multilingual settings. CCP involves learning from CCP samples in contrast to random contexts (RoSS), which often serves as noise. However, CCP samples offer a more accurate representation of context due to their relevance to sentence meaning. Nevertheless, CCP samples are scarce, making it impractical to solely rely on CCP for training. RoSS, on the other hand, is easily accessible but may be less beneficial for training. To resolve this issue, we propose a new method known as CCP-RoSS, which combines CCP and RoSS through a process involving data augmentation and knowledge transfer. Our research demonstrates that CCP-RoSS achieves the best results in zero-shot word vector targeting across 102 languages, particularly for languages with limited training data.

In recent years, researchers have developed numerous multimodal learning methods that have achieved impressive performance in various downstream tasks. However, many of these approaches fail to effectively leverage the distinct characteristics of different modalities, resulting in the dominant modalities overpowering the others. To address this issue, we introduce a novel method, Prototypical Modality Rebalancing (PMR), which utilizes prototypical networks to train multimodal models. By combining the benefits of prototypical networks and multimodal learning techniques, PMR enables the model to capture the shared patterns between modalities while preserving the unique characteristics of each modality. Moreover, PMR provides a computationally efficient way to identify the most informative modality in each task, which is particularly useful when multiple modalities are not available for training. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate that PMR surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in both labeled and unlabeled multimodal learning scenarios.

The kinetic equations for fermions are derived from the quantum field
theoretical functions of one-particle distribution and kinetic operators.
The traditional kinetic equations are obtained when the density variation
between different points is insignificant, which is often indicated by a
constant particle number density. The condition of nonzero density
variation leads to the appearance of an additional term in the kinetic
equation, the divergence of particle density multiplied by the interaction
kernel. The new kinetic equation is then established and the properties
of its solutions are studied. The condition for the existence of a
nonnegative solution of the kinetic equation is examined. The influence
of the particle density divergence on the kinetic equation is then discussed
in more detail. The kinetic equation for the photon gas is solved, and it
is found that in the case of nonzero density variation, the photon
temperature is not equal to the hadron temperature.

In the context of autonomous driving, command and motion forecasting are essential tools. This study focuses on command recognition, a task typically addressed using recurrent neural networks like LSTM. However, recent research has explored the feasibility of replacing these with CNN-based architectures, yielding better performance. This paper presents a command recognition model that integrates the benefits of CNN and recurrent networks, achieving state-of-the-art results. The proposed architecture, CNN+(TT-DNN), consists of a TT-DNN component that processes commands, building on the command features extracted by a CNN. Evaluation using the NPMK dataset demonstrated that the CNN+(TT-DNN) model outperformed a traditional CNN model, offering improved parameter efficiency with a 1.4x parameter reduction while maintaining a command recognition accuracy of 97.7%.

We present a method to control the evolution of a quantum system by exploiting its non-hermitian properties under external driving forces. Our approach reveals that the system can be manipulated in a deterministic manner, including achieving dynamic control over energy transfer, as evidenced by the trimer system's dynamic chiral symmetry breaking. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system's spectrum can be modulated in a deterministic manner via tunable parameters and periodic driving forces. Our findings also indicate that the system's deterministic evolution can be influenced by the nature of its eigenstates, specifically, off-diagonal elements can be introduced and removed by adjusting system parameters and driving frequency. Ultimately, we show that the system's deterministic evolution can be controlled within a specific time frame by fine-tuning its parameters and periodic driving forces.

A method for converting light into electrical current using plasmonic nanoparticles in a scattering-based approach is discussed. By optimizing the geometry of these nanoparticles, their ability to absorb and convert solar energy is analyzed. Results show that a specific design, consisting of a square arrangement of aluminum nanoparticles, can achieve an efficiency of 33.3% by taking into account both scattering and absorption losses. Notably, this performance surpasses that of a standard plasmonic photocell designed to minimize reflection. To validate these findings, simulations based on Maxwell's equations were employed to model the interaction between light and the nanoparticle array.

The combination of an algebra of binary relations and linear-time modal dynamic logic serves as a versatile model of computation, capable of representing various processes such as games, system runs, partial functions, and approximating infinite behaviors. The logic's expression of refinement and hidden actions allows for capturing certain specifications like fairness and determinism, but a detailed formula-based description of these properties is lacking. In our study, we developed a refinement logic for linear-time modal dynamics and utilized it to define fairness and determinism in separate formulas. Furthermore, our findings indicate that these specified properties are not equivalently expressible through other standard modal logic techniques.

Real-world tensor data often exhibit complex structural properties that are essential for accurate predictions. To address this, we've developed a novel approach that combines frequency-domain tensor decomposition with a low-latency, model-free neural network framework. This allows our proposed FDHT-LSTM model to efficiently process and predict time-series tensor data, while also being compatible with advanced neural network accelerators. Through extensive simulations, we've shown that the FDHT-LSTM model offers significant performance improvements, including 10-fold higher throughput and 100-fold better energy efficiency, compared to traditional hardware implementations that rely on tensor decomposition and dedicated accelerators.

This paper presents a secure communication system for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), leveraging the widely-used MAVLink protocol. By encrypting and decrypting messages on the UAV and ground station respectively, the system ensures secure and efficient remote operation of the aircraft. Employing various encryption algorithms, the research finds AES to be the most efficient in securing MAVLink messages, and subsequently, the system is tested in multiple flight experiments to verify its functionality. Notably, the system is capable of supporting real-time MAVLink messaging between the UAV and controller, validated through successful flight tests of a quadcopter.

The complexity of network emulation stems from accurately modeling various interacting components, such as network protocols, devices, and topologies.
